articles.title: Inside Ken Paxton's jet-setting lifestyle: California wineries, European hot spots and ski resorts
articles.summary: When Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton launched his campaign for Senate last year, he skipped the local pageantry.  Instead, records show, the conservative f...
articles.body:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — When Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton launched his campaign for Senate last year, he skipped the local pageantry.

Instead, records show, the conservative firebrand announced his bid on Fox News , cleared his calendar and booked a hotel in Augusta, Georgia, during the storied Masters golf tournament, a trip that cost Texas taxpayers at least $25,000.

The trip reflected a transformation that has unfolded over Paxton's 11 tumultuous years as Texas' top law enforcement official: His focus has increasingly extended beyond state lines. As he steadily built a national political profile and became a star in President Donald Trump's MAGA universe, Paxton traveled frequently and spent less time in Texas, according to an Associated Press review of state and campaign records.

Since assuming office in 2015, Paxton left about 730 workdays blank on his official calendars and took over 275 out-of-state trips to places such as the California wine country, Caribbean resorts and European tourism hot spots. The travel cost Texas taxpayers a minimum of $1.9 million to cover expenses charged by his security detail, records show. It is unclear how Paxton has financed much of his portion of the travel.

The pattern became more pronounced as Paxton became a ubiquitous presence in conservative media and filed a stream of partisan lawsuits to oppose Democratic President Joe Biden's agenda, endearing himself to Trump. Early in his tenure, his official calendars were packed with job-related duties. In 2021, more than 90 workdays were blank — a number that reached 112 in 2024, the last full year the AP had records for.

Texas does not require the attorney general to report his day-to-day whereabouts, and other state records do not often reveal the length or purpose of the out-of-state travel. Texas, however, keeps records for the monthly expenses incurred by his security detail. Those records show reimbursements for travel outside Texas spiked from about $30,000 in 2015 to nearly $400,000 in 2024.

"There is clearly a pattern of behavior here that may make some voters question how seriously Ken Paxton has taken the job," said Joshua Blank, the director of research for the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin. "At the same time, Ken Paxton has been accused of a lot of things and those accusations have not hurt him in any significant way yet."

Paxton's travel has been an issue in campaign

Paxton's record as attorney general and his travel have become an issue in the Senate campaign, a race that could prove pivotal in deciding party control of the chamber.

His Democratic opponent in the November election, James Talarico, criticized Paxton for spending July 4 in Great Britain and accused him of focusing more on his standing in Trump's political movement than on issues facing Texans. In a recent social media post, Talarico chided Paxton for misspelling the name of a Texas town. "It's Cypress, not 'Cyprus,'" Talarico wrote on Sept. 20. "But for all the time you spend on luxury vacations in Europe, it's no surprise you don't know Texas."

The travel has also served as an uncomfortable reminder of Paxton's complicated personal life.

Last year, his primary opponent, Sen. John Cornyn, posted a photo online of Paxton attending the 2024 Kentucky Derby with a group that included a woman who he has since been spotted traveling alone with.

"Quite the unforgettable day for Crooked Ken and Tracy Duhon!" Cornyn wrote , adding, "If you know you know."

Numerous publications have reported that Paxton and Duhon, a Christian influencer and author, have an alleged romantic relationship, though both have declined to publicly address the matter.

Paxton's wife, Texas state Sen. Angela Paxton, filed for divorce last year on "biblical grounds" and accused the attorney general of infidelity. Duhon, who was not named in the Paxtons' divorce filings, did not respond to a request for comment.

Paxton's campaign would not make him available for an interview and declined to comment for this story. Madison Cercy, a Paxton spokeswoman, directed all questions to the Texas Attorney General's office, which did not directly respond to a detailed list of questions about Paxton's travel, including how he pays for it.

In an unsigned statement, Paxton's office said that calendar entries do not "capture someone's full workday, including hours of calls, negotiations, case strategy, and briefings with his team that fill every day."

Paxton's office said he has helped secure large legal settlements from drugmakers and tech companies, which requires routine travel. His office added that Paxton, like other high-profile state officials, travels with a security detail because he faces threats "stemming from his courageous work … fighting on behalf of the people of Texas."

"Attorney General Paxton leads an agency of more than 4,000 employees and is briefed daily on the most pressing matters across the office," the statement reads. "His schedule is built to be immediately responsive to the most pressing issues in order to best serve Texans."

Paxton has been an 'activist' attorney general

Since taking office more than a decade ago, the former state lawmaker and probate lawyer has been under a cloud of scrutiny. Paxton was investigated by the FBI but never charged. Without admitting guilt, he paid restitution to settle a felony securities fraud case brought by state prosecutors. And he was impeached — but later acquitted — by fellow Republicans on accusations of abusing his office and accepting bribes .

He has survived politically thanks to a deep well of support from his Christian conservative base and a close affiliation with Trump. He cemented the bond early in his tenure by turning his office into an operating base for the conservative movement and pursuing litigation to further its goals.

Paxton, for example, spearheaded a failed effort to overturn Trump's 2020 presidential election loss to Biden. After Biden took office, Paxton sued the Democratic administration more than 100 times, a feat he has boasted about on the campaign trail.

Paxton did not invent the "activist" model for attorneys general but marshaled it in a way that enhanced his political brand, said Brandon Rottinghaus, a professor of political science at the University of Houston.

"The culture war litigation became a central function of his office rather than a peripheral one," said Rottinghaus. Paxton, he added, "learned that litigation itself generated political capital."

Tom Phillips, a former Republican chief justice on the Texas Supreme Court, said Paxton's politicization of the office was a factor in his decision to endorse the Democratic candidate, state Sen. Nathan Johnson, in the race to succeed him as attorney general. "The office of attorney general should be conducted in a nonpartisan fashion. Not to advance their own political agenda," said Phillips.

Paxton's evolution into a national political figure can be seen in his official calendars, according to records. Early in his tenure, his schedule was packed with the typical duties of a state attorney general.

For example, during his first year in office, he routinely met with state lawmakers, greeted constituents, delivered speeches and huddled with deputies for strategy meetings.

Over the last five years, the calendars contained few listings of such activities, appearing to confirm what two former deputies told impeachment investigators in 2023: He often skipped meetings and was indifferent to many of his job's day-to-day duties, which were delegated to his top deputies.

"I didn't have a whole lot of contact with Attorney General Paxton," Mark Penley, a former deputy attorney general, told impeachment investigators in 2023. "He was gone a lot, he was traveling, he was out."

Over a two-year period ending in 2024, Paxton flew to the Caribbean , Israel, India, Taiwan, South Africa, made three trips to Europe and hit five different ski towns in the Rockies, including numerous visits to Park City, Utah, among other destinations, records show.

In the summer of 2022, a year in which he was running for reelection, Paxton embarked on a multistop European tour that included visits to Italy, Albania, Greece and Malta, as previously reported by the Dallas Morning News. Paxton also stopped at an Idaho resort town and at Trump's Bedminster golf club in New Jersey, where he held a fundraiser. His travel that year cost the public roughly $230,000 to reimburse members of his security detail, records show.

While the number of blank days included in Paxton's calendars trended upward during his tenure, other patterns emerged , too.

In 2022, for example, Paxton's calendar contained just 79 blank days, but included 96 days in which the only listed activities were interviews he scheduled with conservative media outlets.

The following year his schedule contained more conservative media interviews — 122 — than the 98 events related to the day-to-day operations of his office, records show.

Texas conservatives, including Paxton, have treated California as a punching bag. "Don't California My Texas" is a favorite phrase of Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, who uses it as a pejorative shorthand for the liberal values commonly associated with the west coast state.

Paxton recently took a swipe at the state while attacking his November opponent. "California already has two senators. It doesn't need a third. But that's exactly what James Talarico would be," Paxton said last month when Republicans gathered in Texas for a midterm election summit convened by Trump.

That kind of disdain has not stopped Paxton from spending time in California, where he spent a portion of his youth. Records show Paxton has taken over 25 trips to the state, costing Texas taxpayers over $175,000.

"I like places in California, even though I don't like to admit that I go to California. But it's beautiful," Paxton said on the "Swimming with the Sharks" podcast last November.

He has shown a particular fondness for Northern California's wine country, which he visited at least five times, records show.

In 2019, Paxton used $11,000 from his campaign fund to pay for lodging at a boutique Napa Valley hotel, vineyard tours and stops at two wineries, which he described in campaign finance reports as a fundraising expense. The trip cost taxpayers $8,100 in security costs, records show.

Another wine country visit in 2024 cost the public over $14,000, records show. During the trip, Paxton ventured near Yosemite National Park, records show, where his campaign paid for meals, including $436 dropped at Mammoth Rock Restaurant, a French-inspired brasserie that offers "elevated" classics such as escargot and duck confit.

It's unclear how Paxton has financed most of his jet-setting lifestyle. He tapped his campaign fund to cover expenses in some instances. His Senate campaign and his office did not offer comment on the matter.

Though he was not wealthy when first elected to the legislature in 2002, Paxton's net worth has soared in recent years. A financial disclosure he recently filed with the Senate indicates he has millions of dollars in assets.

But the documents offer an incomplete picture. As attorney general, Paxton makes about $153,000 a year and has said he is not obligated to disclose assets held in a trust. His net worth has fluctuated in the periodic reports he has filed with the Senate, which give values in ranges but do not provide precise dollar figures. A document filed last year indicated he had substantial debts and may have a negative net worth. A disclosure Paxton filed in August indicated he may be worth more than $20 million, much of it related to his growing real estate portfolio .

Since Trump's first election in 2016, Paxton could often be found in Washington, visiting more than 31 times. After Trump began plotting his political comeback following his 2020 election loss, Paxton made regular pilgrimages to Palm Beach, home to Trump's private club, Mar-a-Lago.

In early 2021, when Trump was in political exile for his role in the Jan. 6 Capitol attack, Paxton played a game of golf with him. That same year Paxton paid nearly $50,000 to hold a fundraiser for himself at Mar-a-Lago and flew into West Palm Beach aboard a private jet, according to campaign finance disclosures.

He's since made 11 more visits to the area, records show, in addition to 28 other visits to Florida cities, including two stops at Disney World.

articles.title: The tweet that defined a decade of Trump
articles.summary: Ten years ago, Jesse Farrar produced a tweet that will probably be the most influential piece of writing of his life: “Well, I’d like to see ol Donny Trump w...
articles.body:
Ten years ago, Jesse Farrar produced what will probably be the most influential piece of writing of his life. It was a tweet, fired off casually late in the evening of October 1, 2016. He doesn't even remember what prompted him to do it. "I was probably bored and wanted attention," Farrar admitted.

Farrar's post was a tiny script, of sorts, in which a character makes a pronouncement that is then interrupted by an action denoted by asterisks. It read:

It was a throwaway gag, but it was a throwaway gag with the earth-shaking power of prophecy. Much has been written about the Trump era and the norm-upending, scandal-surviving, attention-craving main character at its center. But few pieces of writing so deftly captured how the political and media cycles would play out over the next 10 years, again and again and again.

Consider this: Farrar posted his tweet six days before news of the "Access Hollywood" tape broke. Before the press began waiting to see when Trump's pious running mate, Mike Pence, would abandon the sordid, disgraced candidate and his obviously doomed campaign. Before — Ah! Well. Nevertheless

It was the tweet that became a meme that became a mantra, a skeleton key that still unlocks the past decade of American life.

"It's indisputably one of the most important tweets in American politics about American politics, particularly from a leftist perspective," said Jake Christie, who has been running a yearslong social media project called the "Museum of Twitter," wherein he analyzes the site's most influential posts, including an episode devoted to Farrar's . "You just see it everywhere."

That's because, thanks to both President Donald Trump's own skills and the institutions around him, the president has been able to wriggle out of a series of jams — investigations and impeachments, charges and convictions — that would have ended the careers of countless other politicians. He lost an election, responded with the most cataclysmic sore-loser performance in American history, then still found his way back to more power than ever before.

And like Farrar's Twitter character, dangling on that final, hopeful comma, the president's critics still return to speculating that this next scandal might just be the one that delivers comeuppance.

"Writing his political obituary is a fool's errand — he endures persecution and eludes prosecution like no other public figure," Kellyanne Conway, Trump's 2016 campaign manager and White House senior adviser, wrote in the New York Times in 2023 . "That cat has nine lives."

For Farrar, now 38, unintentionally becoming the Nostradamus of a surreal and often very dumb political era has been a bizarre experience — haunting, even. Each time he's confronted by his own words in others' online jokes or in news stories, he's reminded of who he was when he first wrote them and what the world used to feel like.

If anything, he wishes his little joke hadn't proved so insightful. "I couldn't have fathomed that we would have been doing it 10 years on, but we keep waiting for something to happen, and I just think it's probably not going to," Farrar said. "The world does keep on spinning like this, and that's why I think it sucks so bad."

Despite his indelible contribution to political discourse, Farrar says he mostly experiences politics vicariously. Living with his wife and three kids in the exurbs of Nashville, he's a leftist in a red state where he has never felt that any party truly represents him.

He's now the co-host of the "Your Kickstarter Sucks" podcast and the "Go Off Kings" Twitch stream , but in 2016 Farrar was still figuring his life out, earning money as a freelancer by writing for places like Deadspin, The Daily Dot and Vice. Many of the outlets he worked with are now gone and Farrar's work scrubbed from the internet.

Like many terminally online people, he recalls finding great humor in watching Trump, someone seemingly as addicted to Twitter as he himself was, campaigning for president. If the world of politics had always seemed like one big joke, here was a candidate who seemed to treat it as such.

At this point 10 years ago, Trump and his campaign had already survived 16 months of crises, from the day he launched his White House bid by calling Mexicans "rapists." There were his disparagements against Sen. John McCain and other prisoners of war , his sexist comments against then-Fox News host Megyn Kelly , his mocking of a New York Times reporter with a disability , his calls for a Muslim ban , his initial resistance to denouncing a former Ku Klux Klan grand wizard , his attacks on a federal judge with Mexican heritage , his feud with a Muslim Gold Star family , and his saying that " Second Amendment people " might be able to "do" something to stop Hillary Clinton abolishing the right to bear arms or that Russian hackers should "find" Clinton's emails.

Each of these scandals generated countless headlines from an aghast press and commentariat class. Trump wriggled out of all of them.

When Farrar wrote his fateful tweet, with the election just weeks away, Trump was caught up in yet another controversy, this one involving a woman named Alicia Machado . A former Miss Universe who had been namechecked by Hillary Clinton in the first debate, Machado said Trump had called her "Miss Piggy" and "Miss Housekeeping" when she had held the beauty pageant crown. He had denied Machado's claims, but then proceeded to blast her in a series of middle-of-the-night tweets posted the day before Farrar's.

Right around the time Farrar hit send, yet another scandal arrived: The New York Times published sections of Trump's tax records , which Trump had refused to release. The documents showed he'd claimed a $916 million loss in 1995 that could have allowed him to avoid any federal income taxes for the next 18 years.

Looking back, Farrar doesn't claim to have any extra political insights about that particular moment in history. He was simply marveling, like much of the country, that Trump seemed to be getting away with things that would previously have been politically unthinkable.

Some 10 months earlier, during a campaign stop in Iowa , Trump had remarked that his supporters were so loyal to him, "I could stand in the middle of Fifth Avenue and shoot somebody, and I wouldn't lose any voters." That joke, which seemed to feel truer with each passing day, prompted Farrar to make his own.

Despite everything that that happened, he didn't really believe Trump was going to win. "I thought it was a good goof," he said. "I wish it had been, certainly."

Here is a non-exhaustive list of the outlets that have referenced Farrar's tweet, sometimes even in headlines, in the years since he wrote it: The New York Times , The Washington Post , The Atlantic , The New Yorker , New York Magazine , Vox , Jezebel , Slate , HuffPost , The New Republic , BuzzFeed News , USA Today , Billboard and Esquire. Naturally, it also has its own entry on the internet anthology Know Your Meme .

McKay Coppins at The Atlantic called it "one of the all-time great tweets of this era," while his colleague David A. Graham said it was of the "essential examples" of memes that make up the Trump era. "At some moment, the tweet transformed from a riposte to naive pundits into a shorthand for the strangeness of American politics," Graham wrote earlier this summer.

"That particular tweet has had a lot of staying power," said Dave Weigel, a political reporter at Semafor who's previously referenced the " history " of Farrar's tweet. "It was pretty perceptive because there's so many liberals who just thought, 'Well, surely he can't get away with this,' but that has atrophied over time."

Weigel recalls covering the 2016 campaign for the Washington Post and never quite believing that the parade of scandals would ultimately be Trump's downfall — especially once he won and had the power of the presidency behind him.

Fervor for Trump was so high among his supporters, and Weigel could sense a desire among some increasingly influential people to push back on what he calls "Watergate Brain": the idea that a candidate, let alone a president, should be forced to face career-ending consequences for wrongdoing. (Vice President JD Vance would agree; in June 2026, he said if the Watergate scandal had occurred today, it would be a 12-hour news story. "The idea that it would have taken down a presidency is crazy," Vance said .)

"I think there's just been an understanding that scandals are not what they used to be," Weigel said. "Trump survived. Is that unique to him?"

I wriggle by with the help of my friends

Analysts have spent much of the last decade trying to define what has made Trump such a unique, seemingly Teflon-clad political creature. For one, he studied under the tutelage of Roy Cohn, where the philosophy, as summed up by acolyte Roger Stone, was always "admit nothing, deny everything, launch counterattack." And, especially in his second term as president, he's clearly adopted the "flood the zone with sh*t" strategy of his early adviser Steve Bannon, correctly assuming the media and general public would struggle to keep up with an avalanche of controversy.

But to assume Trump possesses some sort of "special political magic" may itself be a faulty premise, according to Julia Azari, a political scientist at Wisconsin's Marquette University who has traced the evolution (or devolution) of American political norms.

"He doesn't lose popularity because of these scandals, but he's never all that popular either," said Azari, pointing to polling in which Trump has never really enjoyed a plurality of widespread public support. "I think that we lose a lot of analytical leverage when we write him off as being magical."

Similarly, New York Times columnist Jamelle Bouie told Christie in his "Museum of Twitter" series that Farrar's tweet was "defeatist" because it played into the idea of Trump being the only person with any agency — the "main character of the world" — that everyone else is stuck reacting to.

Instead, Bouie believes it's the people and institutions around Trump — from Republicans to Democrats, Congress to the courts — that have made the last decade possible.

"Other people don't bother to deal with the fact that you could probably get him to go away for good. They kind of allow him to wriggle his way back in," Bouie said. "He's really figured out that persistence is 99% of success. All you have to do is show up and not go away, and people will be like, 'I guess this guy is supposed to be here.'" (White House staff did not respond to a request for comment for this story.)

One skill Trump has shown, though, is a talent for reframing his scandals to convince his supporters that outrage about his behavior is part of broader liberal hostility toward them, according to Whitney Phillips at the University of Oregon who has written books about polarization and "anti-liberal demonology." Farrar's tweet, Phillips said, plays off the dynamic of liberals getting up in arms, and people then making fun of liberals for getting up in arms.

Some of this liberal zeal, which Farrar was mocking from a leftist perspective, has been stoked by online actors or cable news talking heads who constantly tease new developments in ongoing Trump-in-trouble narratives to build hope and their own audience numbers. (Remember those Robert Mueller prayer candles ?)

But some of it is also an inevitable byproduct of the media doing their job by investigating potential wrongdoing. "Even if all of the coverage from the very beginning had absolutely been 100% straight news reporting with no editorializing and no giddiness, then it still would have been sucked into this narrative of Trump's, where any opposition makes you partisan," Phillips said. "That's just this amazing trick that he has mastered."

For Farrar, seeing his own words used to this day in stories that tease whether the end may finally be nigh can be uniquely exhausting. When Graham, The Atlantic writer, used Farrar's tweet in a July story about the Iran war being the "trap" that has finally dealt a blow to Trump's sheen of invincibility, Farrar was unmoved. "Where's the trap? Is he caught yet? Is it over? Nothing happened," Farrar said.

Even as Republicans distance themselves from an increasingly unpopular Trump ahead of the midterms, and even as Democrats prepare themselves for the potential for sweeping victories that could deliver them power in Congress, Farrar remains gloomy. He has no faith that they or anyone else will suddenly hold the president to account, nor that the president will cease doing whatever he pleases.

Farrar acknowledged Bouie's criticism that his attitude was defeatist; he is defeatist. And cynical. And jaded. Being the unintentional voice of political pessimism can make a person something of a pessimist.

Over 10 years, he's been taught to be skeptical that consequences or karma still exist for some. The system, as he sees it, is rigged towards elite impunity, and nothing in the last decade has proved him wrong yet.

"I think if you keep betting on 'Nothing happens,' you're only wrong once, and then it's like, 'Well, great. I'm glad I was wrong," Farrar said. "But until then, I've racked up a million victories on 'Bad things don't happen to powerful people.' That's how the world is organized, you know."

articles.title: Musk’s AI chatbot Grok reportedly encouraged Trump to capture  Venezuela’s president
articles.summary: President Trump reportedly asked for Grok's opinion before invading Venezuela and capturing Nicolás Maduro.
articles.body:
In December 2025, about a month before the U.S. invaded Venezuela and captured its president, Nicolás Maduro, President Trump had a secret meeting with Elon Musk, Time magazine reports. This was roughly seven months after Musk left his role in the Trump administration at the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

During this meeting, Trump "spent hours" talking to Musk's Grok chatbot, including asking how Venezuelans would respond to the capture of their president, a source told Time. Just a few months earlier, in September, Trump began ordering U.S. military strikes against Venezuelan boats that Trump alleged were involved in drug trafficking.

People had apparently been turning to Grok asking about the boat strikes and political climate in Venezuela, as The Atlantic reported at the time. So Grok told Trump that Maduro was a "deeply unpopular dictator and that many Venezuelans would likely celebrate his downfall," Time reported.

When such celebrations indeed happened after the U.S. invaded on January 3, Trump apparently "came away thinking Grok was ingenious," that source told Time.

So perhaps it should come as no surprise that in June of this year, the Pentagon's head of AI said that the military used Grok Gov to deploy and strike targets during the Iran War.

While Grok isn't the only AI model serving the DoD (OpenAI also has an agreement and Anthropic has been in a back-and-forth over how its models can be used for military intelligence and in modern warfare ), Grok may become an even bigger favorite under this administration. Earlier this week, the Pentagon announced that Musk and Anduril's Palmer Luckey have been tapped to co-lead a study about how advanced technology is, and can be, used in battlefields.

articles.title: Judiciário nas eleições: análise do impacto do TSE e STF no 1º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Decisões do TSE e do STF influenciam estratégias de campanha, esvaziam debate presidencial e reforçam a judicialização de uma eleição marcada por embates nos tribunais.
articles.summary: O Judiciário nas eleições assumiu papel central com decisões do TSE e STF que alteraram estratégias de Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro, resultando no cancelamento de debates.
articles.body:
A reta final da campanha para o primeiro turno foi marcada menos pelo confronto de propostas entre os candidatos e mais pela atuação do Judiciário, que se consolidou como protagonista da disputa eleitoral. Em poucas horas, decisões do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE) e do Supremo Tribunal Federal ( STF ) impactaram diretamente as estratégias dos adversários e redefiniram o cenário político.

Nos bastidores da campanha do presidente Lula ( PT ), a preocupação central era o impacto de sua ausência no debate promovido pela Globo. Depois de comunicar que não participaria do encontro , a equipe do petista temia que os adversários explorassem a imagem de um púlpito vazio, especialmente o candidato Flávio Bolsonaro ( PL ).

A campanha recorreu ao TSE, que acabou determinando a retirada do púlpito , decisão que ajudou a neutralizar uma das armas dos oponentes.

Do lado de Flávio Bolsonaro, a reação foi imediata. Inicialmente decidido a comparecer ao debate mesmo sem a presença de Lula, o candidato mudou de estratégia após as decisões judiciais. A campanha comunicou interferência do Judiciário no processo eleitoral e de alinhamento institucional favorável ao presidente, narrativa que ganhou força entre aliados e alimentou a mobilização da reta final.

O episódio é mais um capítulo de uma eleição em que os tribunais ocuparam espaço central no debate público. Ao longo da campanha, questões judiciais, decisões de ministros e disputas internas nas cortes frequentemente se sobrepuseram às discussões sobre programas de governo e propostas para o país.

A influência do Judiciário vai além dos episódios eleitorais imediatos. As movimentações dentro do STF e do TSE refletem também disputas por poder e sobrevivência política nas próprias instituições, em um contexto em que os resultados das urnas e a futura composição do Senado são acompanhados de perto pelos magistrados . Assim, às vésperas da votação, o Judiciário chega ao primeiro turno como um dos principais personagens da corrida eleitoral.

articles.title: Brasil investiga ameaça que fechou embaixada e consulados dos EUA | G1
articles.standfirst: Gestão Trump suspendeu atividades nas representações diplomáticas alegando questões de segurança, mas não detalhou razões. Auxiliares de Lula afirmam que Brasil já apurava supostas ameaças antes da divulgação do comunicado norte-americano sobre suspensão.
articles.summary: A Embaixada dos EUA suspendeu serviços por segurança, e o governo brasileiro investiga a natureza das ameaças que também afetaram a representação da Austrália no país.
articles.body:
O governo brasileiro apura o que seria a "possível ameaça" apontada pelos Estados Unidos como motivo para suspender o atendimento na embaixada norte-americana em Brasília e em consulados no Brasil nesta quinta-feira (1º).

Autoridades ouvidas pelo g1 não confirmam a natureza dos indícios, alegando que isso pode comprometer a averiguação da situação. E afirmam que neste momento é melhor "errar por excesso do que por omissão".

Um auxiliar do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva ( PT ) afirmou ao g1 que as autoridades brasileiras estão atentas para esse caso, mas que não é preciso alarde .

Nesta quinta-feira (1º), o governo norte-americano divulgou um comunicado suspendendo o atendimento presencial na Embaixada dos EUA em Brasília e nos consulados do país em todo o Brasil nesta sexta-feira (2) por questões de segurança.

O governo dos EUA não deixou claro que tipo de serviços consulares fornecidos pela embaixada foram suspensos. Também não especificou se seguirá emitindo vistos e passaportes no período.

Segundo interlocutores do governo brasileiro, os EUA comunicaram o Brasil sobre os indícios de ameaça e as autoridades brasileiras já estavam investigando o caso antes da divulgação do comunicado sobre o fechamento da embaixada norte-americana .

Existe uma cooperação entre autoridades brasileira e norte-americanas na área de segurança.

Nesta manhã, a Embaixada da Austrália anunciou que ficará fechada ao longo desta sexta-feira (2). Em um comunicado, o governo australiano também alegou "'questões de segurança".

De acordo com fontes do governo brasileiro, não há indícios de ameaças sobre a embaixada da Austrália até o momento. A Austrália decidiu fechar as portas se baseando na decisão dos EUA, informaram.

articles.title: Por que a nova onda de protestos estudantis assusta o governo francês | G1
articles.standfirst: Um movimento que começou há quase duas semanas se espalhou. E na França, jovens protestando nas ruas significam problemas para o governo.
articles.summary: Um movimento que começou há quase duas semanas se espalhou. E na França, jovens protestando nas ruas significam problemas para o governo.
articles.body:
Desde os famosos protestos de 1968, os governos franceses sempre reconheceram o poder dos jovens que vão às ruas — Foto: AFP via Getty Images

É um conselho sábio que todos os líderes franceses fazem questão de seguir: jovens nas ruas são sinônimo de problemas.

Desde os protestos estudantis de maio de 1968 — descritos de forma memorável pelo presidente Charles De Gaulle como "chienlit" (literalmente "defecação na cama", ou seja, caos) – todos os governos têm medo da juventude francesa revoltada.

Por quê? Porque os movimentos juvenis são imprevisíveis e amorfos, muitas vezes sem uma estrutura clara com a qual se possa negociar. Porque quando eles protestam, outros grupos se juntam a eles.

Além disso, como são jovens, o público tende a simpatizar com eles. E porque, se a polícia errar e provocar ferimentos ou algo pior, as consequências são incalculáveis. E as eleições presidenciais estão a poucos meses de distância.

Por todas essas razões, quando a juventude revoltada está nas barricadas, os governos agem com muita cautela.

Neste momento, os adolescentes franceses estão nas barricadas e, embora não estejam visivelmente revoltados (o clima é mais de excitação), certamente estão deixando o governo do presidente Emmanuel Macron "apavorado", segundo descrição do jornal Le Monde.

Um movimento que começou há quase duas semanas na área de baixa renda de Seine-Saint-Denis, no norte de Paris, espalhou-se por todo o país nos últimos dias.

Na quinta-feira (1/10) – o ponto mais crítico até agora – centenas de liceus (escolas onde jovens de 15 a 18 anos concluem seus estudos) estavam sendo bloqueados. Na sexta-feira, a situação havia melhorado, mas cerca de 400 liceus permaneceram fechados para proteger funcionários e alunos. As universidades estão começando a seguir o exemplo.

A violência eclodiu. Na quinta-feira, o salão principal de um liceu em Nantes foi destruído por um incêndio. Incêndios menores, numerosos demais para mencionar, foram provocados nos portões de entrada de escolas em todo o país. O prejuízo estimado é de milhões de euros.

Segundo o Ministro da Educação, Édouard Geffray, 65 membros do corpo docente, incluindo 40 diretores de escolas, ficaram feridos.

"A maioria dos funcionários feridos afirmou que as pessoas com quem se depararam... não eram seus próprios alunos", disse ele.

Os protestos se espalharam por toda a França, e alguns estudantes universitários agora estão se juntando a eles — Foto: AFP via Getty Images

Além disso, o governo afirma que cerca de 300 policiais e bombeiros receberam atendimento médico devido aos ferimentos, e aproximadamente 2 mil pessoas – principalmente menores de idade – foram detidas. Por sua vez, grupos estudantis relatam ter uma longa lista de pessoas feridas pela polícia. Dois adolescentes sofreram graves lesões oculares e um perdeu vários dentes.

O problema já seria bastante complexo se se resumisse apenas a atender às reivindicações dos manifestantes. Mas existe outra dimensão – política e social – que torna esta crise estudantil muito mais perigosa do que no passado.

As reivindicações existem, ainda que permaneçam vagas. Elas dizem respeito à falta de dinheiro e à necessidade de mais professores, turmas menores e melhores instalações.

Em relação a esses assuntos, muitos na França concordariam com os adolescentes. Certamente, usar protestos para exigir verbas do governo é um hábito tão arraigado no país que até mesmo os governos o consideram legítimo. E, de fato, a situação no sistema educacional está piorando, devido à escassez de recursos.

Esta semana, o primeiro-ministro Sébastien Lecornu publicou sua proposta de orçamento para o próximo ano. O lema é "Mais cortes – e desta vez é sério!".

Resta saber se ele conseguirá ou não retirar 54 bilhões de euros dos gastos públicos, como promete.

Mas é óbvio que a era da generosidade pública para apaziguar a agitação social na França está agora no fim. Os estudantes que exigem uma enfermeira escolar extra ou isolamento térmico no refeitório provavelmente ficarão decepcionados.

O temor muito maior é que esses protestos estudantis estejam sendo manipulados pela extrema esquerda – e que a violência dos últimos dias seja um prenúncio do que aguarda uma sociedade perigosamente polarizada no ano das eleições que se aproxima.

Bally Bagayoko (à esquerda) e o candidato presidencial Jean-Luc Mélenchon manifestaram apoio ao direito dos estudantes de protestar — Foto: Getty Images

Para a direita e o centro, não há dúvida de que por trás dos problemas estudantis está a mão astuta do partido França Insubmissa (LFI) e de seu popular candidato à presidência, Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

Líderes da LFI têm aparecido regularmente ao lado dos estudantes – principalmente no subúrbio parisiense de Saint-Denis, cujo prefeito, Bally Bagayoko, foi criticado por dizer que "a violência às vezes pode ser legítima".

Um relatório interno preparado para o departamento de polícia de Paris, que vazou para a mídia, analisou o movimento em Seine-Saint-Denis. A conclusão foi de que os estudantes estavam sendo "incitados por elementos de extrema esquerda de grêmios estudantis... e grupos políticos como... a LFI".

O comunicado afirmava que as tensões "poderiam fazer parte de uma estratégia para inflamar os ânimos... com o objetivo de impor suas ideias antes das eleições nacionais".

Para sustentar sua conclusão, os autores do relatório citaram a presença de manifestantes que não são eles próprios estudantes do ensino médio, a imprecisão das reivindicações, o hasteamento de bandeiras palestinas e argelinas e o uso de táticas – como a convocação de protestos suplementares em delegacias de polícia – que fazem parte do manual da esquerda radical.

A LFI nega veementemente ter feito algo além de oferecer seu apoio natural a um movimento que considera legítimo. Na quinta-feira, Mélenchon pediu aos estudantes que evitassem a violência, "que só serve aos interesses de nossos inimigos".

Mas seus oponentes acreditam que o veterano de 75 anos – que tem boas chances de chegar ao segundo turno das eleições presidenciais em maio, provavelmente contra a candidata de extrema-direita Marine Le Pen – sabe exatamente o que está fazendo.

As pesquisas mostram que ele tem um apoio massivo – cerca de 40% – entre os jovens de 18 a 24 anos na França, e que esse apoio se concentra nos subúrbios populosos e com alta imigração das cidades.

Mas os jovens também são os que mais se abstêm nas eleições francesas, então a estratégia – à medida que as eleições se aproximam – será a de dar lembretes constantes a essa parcela da população de que a LFI está ao seu lado e que o seu voto pode contar.

Se isso será suficiente para garantir a vitória de Mélenchon é outra questão. Ele certamente deve levar a sério as pesquisas, que mostram uma derrota esmagadora para Le Pen em um segundo turno.

Se isso acontecer, a França estará em um território muito instável – e os protestos dos jovens nos últimos dias terão sido, de fato, um presságio disso.

articles.title: IA nas eleições 2026: 25% dos ataques a candidatas usam a tecnologia | G1
articles.standfirst: Um em cada quatro imagens ofensivas publicados no X contra candidatas tem sinais de inteligência artificial. Relatório mostra que tecnologia é usada não para enganar o eleitor, mas para ampliar ataques misóginos, transfóbicos, gordofóbicos e racistas.
articles.summary: Estudo revela que a IA nas eleições 2026 impulsiona a violência política de gênero com ataques misóginos e racistas produzidos em massa contra candidatas.
articles.body:
A inteligência artificial (IA) ganhou espaço em uma nova frente da disputa eleitoral: a produção em escala de imagens ofensivas contra mulheres na política. Levantamento do projeto MonitorA, observatório de violência política de gênero nas redes sociais, identificou indícios de uso de IA em 25% das imagens classificadas como ataques ou insultos dirigidos a candidatas no X.

Outros 9% dos casos ficaram em uma zona de incerteza, em que os pesquisadores não conseguiram determinar se houve ou não manipulação por inteligência artificial.

IA em imagens ofensivas contra candidatas no X — Foto: Arte/g1

O dado vem de uma análise de 11.137 imagens publicadas em 9.393 comentários em perfis de 132 candidatas monitoradas durante dois momentos da campanha eleitoral: a largada da disputa, entre 16 e 24 de agosto, e o período posterior à crise envolvendo o Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) e o caso Master, de 2 a 11 de setembro. Ao todo, 660 imagens foram classificadas como ofensivas contra candidatas no X.

Diferentemente do temor tradicional envolvendo deepfakes e desinformação, os pesquisadores concluíram que a maior parte das imagens não tenta se passar por real. São charges, memes, montagens e falsos materiais de campanha produzidos para humilhar, ridicularizar ou desumanizar as candidatas .

🔎 Deepfake é uma manipulação sofisticada da imagem ou da voz de alguém feita com inteligência artificial.

"Esses usos de montagens e imagens sintéticas de baixa qualidade indicam que, nesses casos, não há necessariamente uma intenção de simular a realidade. A IA aparece, sobretudo, como mais uma ferramenta para a produção e disseminação de conteúdos ofensivos", resume o relatório.

O estudo diferencia os conteúdos ofensivos em duas categorias: ataques ou insultos. Insultos são ofensas com linguagem hostil, mais dura que uma crítica, mas que não recorrem diretamente a marcadores de desigualdade, como gênero, raça ou religião. O estudo encontrou 269 imagens com insultos às candidatas.

Já os ataques buscam inferiorizar e deslegitimar candidatas com base em características de grupos historicamente marginalizados, como gênero, raça, sexualidade, deficiência ou religião. O levantamento identificou 391 conteúdos classificados como ataque . Por seu caráter discriminatório, segundo o MonitorA, esses ataques deveriam ser removidos pelas plataformas.

A candidata que concentrou o maior volume de ataques e insultos foi Marina Silva (Rede), com 125 registros ofensivos. Em seguida aparecem Sâmia Bomfim (111) e Erika Hilton (109), ambas do PSOL. Juntas, elas responderam por quase metade de todas as imagens ofensivas encontradas pela pesquisa.

A pesquisa mostra que cada candidata acaba associada a um repertório específico de violências . Além disso, aponta ataques e insultos a candidatas de diferentes lados do espectro político.

Com Sâmia Bomfim, do PSOL, predominam conteúdos gordofóbicos. Segundo o estudo, 70,6% dos ataques contra a parlamentar foram classificados nessa categoria.

Já Erika Hilton, também do PSOL, é alvo de ataques transfóbicos. Quase metade das ofensas recebidas por ela (47,9%) se enquadra nessa categoria. Os conteúdos incluem referências à negação da identidade de gênero e reforço de narrativas transfóbicas.

Marina Silva (Rede), por sua vez, concentra ataques misóginos, desumanizantes e etaristas. Em diversas imagens, a candidata aparece representada como animais, alienígenas ou com uma aparência envelhecida artificialmente. Sozinha, ela é alvo de 17% de todos os ataques e insultos direcionados às candidatas monitoradas.

Quando os pesquisadores classificaram os ataques por categoria, a misoginia apareceu em 99 imagens. Em seguida vieram gordofobia (55), transfobia (46), desumanização (39) e racismo (27).

O estudo destaca dois casos de candidatas da direita, ambas do PL: Julia Zanatta e Vanessa da Silva (conhecida também como Negona do Bolsonaro).

Durante os períodos de análise, Zanatta recebeu 76 registros ofensivos, mas distribuídos de forma desigual: 72 deles foram no segundo período, após viralização de imagens e vídeos relacionados à candidata. As ofensas tinham dois eixos centrais: a sexualização da candidata (com imagens dela de biquíni e comentários que insinuavam um interesse por ela) e questionamentos sobre sua identidade política (associando a candidata a um "falso conservadorismo").

Já Vanessa da Silva foi alvo de 30 imagens ofensivas; 70% delas contendo ataques racistas, com imagens que faziam referência ao período escravocrata.

O relatório faz um paralelo dessas duas candidatas: enquanto Júlia aparece com ofensas sexualizantes, Vanessa é retratada como escravizada e em posts associando a um sentimento de nojo.

O relatório argumenta que, embora o debate público tenha concentrado atenção nos riscos da IA na criação de deepfakes realistas, o fenômeno observado na campanha de 2026 também aponta para outro caminho: o uso da inteligência artificial como ferramenta de produção em massa de memes ofensivos, sátiras agressivas e campanhas de humilhação direcionadas a mulheres candidatas.

articles.title: Após aviso dos EUA, embaixada da Austrália também anuncia fechamento por questões de segurança | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo a Secretaria de Segurança Pública do DF, a Polícia Federal pediu reforço no policiamento da região das embaixadas em Brasília.
articles.summary: Segundo a Secretaria de Segurança Pública do DF, a Polícia Federal pediu reforço no policiamento da região das embaixadas em Brasília.
articles.body:
Comunicado Embaixada da Austrália — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

A embaixada da Austrália no Brasil emitiu um comunicado informando que estará fechada nesta sexta-feira (2) "devido a preocupações com a segurança".

Os EUA suspenderam nessa quinta-feira (1º) o atendimento presencial na Embaixada em Brasília e nos consulados em todo o país. O comunicado não informa o que motivou a decisão.

"Aconselhamos os australianos a também evitarem a Embaixada, os Consulados e as instalações diplomáticas dos EUA no Brasil e áreas adjacentes".

Segundo a Secretaria de Segurança Pública do DF, a Polícia Federal (PF) pediu reforço no policiamento da região das embaixadas em Brasília.

No comunicado completo publicado no site do governo australiano, a embaixada cita a proximidade das eleições deste ano.

"O terrorismo é uma ameaça mundial. Ataques terroristas podem ocorrer em qualquer lugar e a qualquer momento. Esteja atento a possíveis ameaças, especialmente em locais públicos. Terroristas podem ter como alvo áreas turísticas ou outros locais frequentados por estrangeiros e onde grandes multidões possam se reunir", diz a publicação.

O texto prossegue: "O primeiro turno das eleições gerais no Brasil ocorrerá em 4 de outubro. O segundo turno está marcado para 25 de outubro. A cerimônia de posse presidencial será realizada em Brasília no dia 5 de janeiro de 2027. Poderão ocorrer comícios políticos, manifestações e aumento das medidas de segurança antes, durante e depois das eleições".

A nota recomenda cautela para os cidadãos australianos em território brasileiro: "Continuamos a recomendar extrema cautela no Brasil devido à ameaça de crimes violentos".

Para assistência consular urgente, os canais de contato são os telefones do Centro de Emergência Consular em Camberra: +61 2 6261 3305 (do exterior) e 1300 555 135 (dentro da Austrália).

articles.title: Presidente do TSE, Nunes Marques fará pronunciamento em rede nacional na véspera do 1º turno | G1
articles.standfirst: Manifestação do presidente da Corte Eleitoral é praxe antes do pleito. Objetivo é incentivar eleitores a irem às urnas no próximo domingo (4).
articles.summary: Manifestação do presidente da Corte Eleitoral é praxe antes do pleito. Objetivo é incentivar eleitores a irem às urnas no próximo domingo (4).
articles.body:
O ministro Kassio Nunes Marques, presidente do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), fará um pronunciamento em rede nacional de televisão e rádio neste sábado (3), véspera do primeiro turno das eleições.

A manifestação do presidente da Corte Eleitoral é praxe na véspera do pleito. O objetivo é incentivar os brasileiros a irem às urnas no domingo, e exercer a obrigação com o voto.

O ministro também deve apresentar as medidas adotadas pela Justiça Eleitoral para garantir a transparência e segurança do processo e também a participação do eleitor.

Embora o domicílio eleitoral do ministro seja em Teresina (PI), Nunes Marques pediu voto em trânsito para votar em Brasília.

Nunes Marques em sessão plenária do TSE — Foto: Antonio Augusto/TSE

No próximo domingo, dia 4 de outubro, o eleitor brasileiro vai fazer seis escolhas nas urnas para as Eleições 2026.

No primeiro turno, o eleitor deverá seguir a seguinte ordem:

Primeiro, vota para deputado federal (quatro dígitos).

Em seguida, é a vez de votar para deputado estadual ou distrital, no caso do DF (cinco dígitos).

Na sequência, aparece a tela para votar na primeira vaga para senador (três dígitos).

Assim que a urna computar este voto, o eleitor vota novamente para senador (três dígitos).

Na sequência, escolhe o governador do seu estado (dois dígitos).

E, por fim, vota para presidente da República (dois dígitos).

A cada etapa, confira os dados que aparecem na tela, como a foto do candidato, o nome, o número e o partido, antes de apertar a tecla verde de “Confirma” e passar para o próximo cargo em disputa.

❗ATENÇÃO: ao votar nas duas vagas para o Senado, para que os dois votos sejam válidos, é necessário escolher nomes diferentes. Se o eleitor repetir e confirmar o mesmo candidato nas duas opções, o segundo voto será anulado.

No dia da eleição, é possível levar um cola eleitoral já com a ordem de votação na urna para ajudar o eleitor ao fazer suas escolhas. No entanto, esta cola deve ser de papel. Não é permitido usar celular na cabine de votação e este deve ficar no local indicado pelos mesários enquanto o eleitor vota.

articles.title: Trump team is now looking to see if DOJ committed misconduct in investigating Richard Nixon’s Watergate
articles.summary: A burglary at the Watergate complex in June 1972 would ultimately lead to a corruption scandal in Washington and the resignation of President Richard Nixon
articles.body:
The Department of Justice is examining allegations of misconduct by Nixon-era special prosecutors in the Watergate scandal.

Former Nixon aide Geoff Shepard recently presented internal documents to the DOJ’s Office of Professional Responsibility, claiming special prosecutors violated defendants' due process rights during the Watergate investigation.

President Richard Nixon resigned in 1974 amid allegations of obstruction of justice and abuse of power related to the Watergate scandal, with Vice President JD Vance drawing parallels between Nixon and President Donald Trump.

President Donald Trump 's Department of Justice is now looking to see if Nixon-era special prosecutors committed misconduct in investigating the Watergate scandal.

An early morning burglary at the Democratic National Committee's headquarters in the Watergate office complex in Washington, D.C., in June 1972 would become a two-year affair, uncovering corruption inside the White House that would ultimately lead to Republican President Richard Nixon's resignation .

More than 50 years later, Geoff Shepard, a former Nixon aide who has written books on Watergate, was invited last month to give a two-hour presentation to the DOJ's Office of Professional Responsibility, an internal watchdog created out of the Watergate scandal, on allegations that the special prosecutor's office that investigated the break-in committed misconduct, people familiar with the matter told The Wall Street Journal .

A DOJ spokesperson confirmed to The Independent that Shepherd gave a presentation to the Office of Professional Responsibility, but said it does not mean an investigation has been opened.

"OPR declined Mr. Shepherd's request to open an investigation in 2022 under the previous administration. Given his expertise and scholarship on Watergate, he was recently invited to give a presentation to OPR, but that presentation does not constitute an investigation," the spokesperson said.

"OPR remains focused on ensuring that Department attorneys meet the highest professional standards."

Shepard showed DOJ officials internal documents from the Watergate Special Prosecution Force, the Journal reported. Special prosecutor Archibald Cox first led the team and then Leon Jaworski after Nixon demanded Cox be fired.

Shepard claims Cox and Jaworski violated defendants' due process rights in the Watergate investigation by secretly meeting with judges overseeing their cases and suppressing evidence from their legal teams, according to the Journal .

Nixon resigned in August 1974 while facing impeachment for allegations of obstruction of justice, abuse of power and contempt of Congress — mostly in relation to accusations that his administration tried to cover up its involvement in the Watergate break-in.

Speaking at the Richard Nixon Presidential Library in California in June, Vice President JD Vance drew parallels between Nixon and President Donald Trump, who has been indicted multiple times and claimed it was the result of a witch hunt.

"If you look at the story of how the deep state took down Richard Nixon, it's not all that different from what the same groups of people, the same institutions tried to do to Donald Trump in the first Trump administration," Vance said.

He also theorized that if the Watergate scandal were to happen in today's media landscape, it wouldn't impact the White House as greatly as it did in Nixon's time.

"If Watergate happened tomorrow, it would be like a 12-hour news story. The idea that it would have taken down a presidency is crazy," Vance said.

articles.title: La posible fecha de elecciones generales que podría marcar Pedro Sánchez: plazos y cuándo sería la votación
articles.standfirst: Las próximas votaciones, antes de lo esperado
articles.summary: Las próximas votaciones, antes de lo esperado
articles.body: Las tensiones entre el Gobierno de España y sus socios podrían acabar dinamitando antes de lo previsto la actual legislatura. Si bien las elecciones generales estaban previstas para el próximo 2027, lo ocurrido estos días con el decreto de la vivienda y la negativa de Junts a dar los votos necesarios, podría acabar provocando que Pedro Sánchez se vea obligado a convocar elecciones anticipadas. Según una información de elDiario.es, el presidente del Ejecutivo planea convocar elecciones generales para el próximo 29 de noviembre, y es que las presiones y discrepancias entre PSOE y Sumar, además de la falta de apoyos, han derivado en una crisis que podría acelerar todos los plazos. No obstante, en caso de que los comicios se produzcan en la fecha mencionada, a más tardar debería aparecer en el Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE) el próximo 6 de octubre. Ese sería el día límite establecido por la ley debido a los tiempos que deben transcurrir entre el anuncio, la convocatoria y la fecha elegida para los comicios. Mientras se va despejando el horizonte, cabe señalar que los comicios, en caso de no anticiparse, también tienen una fecha tope para celebrarse. Dado que las anteriores tuvieron lugar el 23 de julio de 2023, el Gobierno de España debería convocar las elecciones generales antes del 22 de agosto de 2027 y realizar el decreto de convocatoria el 28 de junio. Los rumores, en todo caso, apuntan a que si no se adelantan y se acaban celebrando el próximo año, lo más probable es que se produjeran entre marzo y abril, dado que en mayo están previstas las elecciones autonómicas y municipales, las cuales se celebrarán el 23 de mayo y no se espera que ambas votaciones coincidan. Sea como fuere, los próximos días pueden ser cruciales para conocer el destino político de España.

articles.title: 'Better to die with self-respect': Former maharaja of Bharatpur Vishvendra Singh quits Congress
articles.summary: JAIPUR: Former Rajasthan minister and former Bharatpur Maharaja Vishvendra Singh on Friday announced that he was leaving the Congress, two days after
articles.body: JAIPUR: Former Rajasthan minister and former Bharatpur Maharaja Vishvendra Singh on Friday announced that he was leaving the Congress, two days after launching a sharp attack on state party president Govind Singh Dotasra over the recent urban local body elections, news agency PTI reported.Singh, a member of the erstwhile Bharatpur royal family, announced his decision in a social media post, saying he was guided by his conscience and was hurt by statements made by some party leaders.However, there was no immediate confirmation from the Congress on whether Singh had formally submitted his resignation."I have always taken decisions in my life by listening to my revered Giriraj Maharaj and my inner voice," Singh said.He said statements made by some "petty and so-called leaders" had angered his supporters and left him hurt."If speaking the truth and not supporting what is wrong and false are sins, I will commit one every time. I neither do wrong nor tolerate wrong," he said.Singh said he had devoted his life to the party but could no longer go ahead with its "wrong policies"."Instead of dying of suffocation, it is better to die with self-respect," Singh said.His announcement came amid a public war of words between him and sections of the state Congress. Singh had earlier blamed the Congress's Bharatpur and Deeg district presidents for the party's performance in the civic polls, alleging that tickets were distributed to favourites while genuine workers were sidelined.Congress won 3,613 wards out of the total declared wards in the civic body polls, compared with 4,179 wards won by the BJP.Singh subsequently targeted Dotasra directly and demanded his resignation. He also sought an investigation into allegations relating to recruitment examinations and benefits allegedly received by members of the PCC chief's family.Dotasra on Thursday rejected suggestions of a rift in the Congress and described reports of differences as part of the BJP's "toolkit"."There is no discord among us. This is the BJP's toolkit. The BJP spreads propaganda and tries to show that there are differences within the Congress," Dotasra had said.Singh is a former Deeg-Kumher MLA who served as tourism minister in the previous Ashok Gehlot government. articles.title: Man charged with cyberstalking Katie Miller
articles.summary: A Massachusetts man was arrested Thursday and charged with cyberstalking conservative podcaster Katie Miller, the wife of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, after prosecutors alleged that he repeatedly called and texted her for weeks. John Anthony Proia III, 41, was indicted on one count of cyberstalking over what prosecutors described as a…
articles.body:
A Massachusetts man was arrested Thursday and charged with cyberstalking conservative podcaster Katie Miller, the wife of White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, after prosecutors alleged that he repeatedly called and texted her for weeks.

John Anthony Proia III, 41, was indicted on one count of cyberstalking over what prosecutors described as a weeks-long harassment campaign between Aug. 3 and Sept. 23, when he sent threatening messages and left numerous vulgar voicemails to Katie Miller, her husband and her parents.

According to the Justice Department, some of the messages sent to her parents described her husband as “evil” and a “Jewish Nazi/white supremacist.”

Court documents did not identify Miller by name and instead described the victim as a former political adviser and prominent Republican figure married to a high-ranking government official. Numerous outlets including The Associated Press cited sources briefed on the case that confirmed she was the alleged victim.

Proia, who comes from the Boston suburb Waltham, pleaded not guilty to the felony charge before a magistrate judge in an initial court appearance.

“As alleged in the Indictment, the defendant repeatedly and relentlessly targeted the victim, her husband and her family with deeply disturbing communications that profoundly disrupted their lives,” U.S. Attorney Leah Foley said in a statement.

“Those who use technology to harass, intimidate or torment others should understand that attempts to anonymize their criminal conduct will not shield them from prosecution,” she added.

Attorney General Todd Blanche also weighed in on the case Thursday, writing on the social platform X that the alleged conduct was “criminal and will be treated as it should — with prosecution!”

Miller shared her gratitude over the arrest and charges in a social media post .

“Thank you Todd Blanche, Leah Foley, and the FBI Washington Field Office for keeping me and my family safe,” she wrote. “Good to see a Boston grand jury indict this man.”

articles.title: Trump’s taxpayer-funded propaganda is blatantly illegal
articles.summary: Trump has already spent $2.5 million running these ads, of your taxpayer dollars. Before he’s done, he’s planning to spend at least 20 million on them.
articles.body:
Over the last few weeks, President Trump has crossed yet another Rubicon. No doubt encouraged by the Supreme Court’s very bad decision exempting him from ever being criminally charged for his conduct as president, he has started simply ignoring the law, especially when his ego is at stake.

It started with his decision to kick CNN, MSNOW and Politico off the White House grounds. Trump explained he banned them because, “They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want try and to diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration.” He later added , “It’s sick. There’s something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories.”

If you are not a lawyer, it might be hard to process just how shocking this behavior is. But take it from me, it’s really bad . Even if you are not a lawyer, you can appreciate that the U.S. government should not punish people — not even the tiniest bit — for saying unflattering things about the president, much less about the president’s political party.

Although Trump’s shamelessness is new, his efforts to punish media outlets he dislikes isn’t. The Associated Press, partially barred from White House events because they refuse to update their style manual to require everyone to refer to “The Gulf of America,” is still in a legal battle with the administration over the ban.

A court quickly ordered the White House to restore access for CNN, MS NOW and Politico. Despite that order, Trump still has it in for CNN, which now finds itself barred from covering the president when he travels.

This week, Trump began releasing taxpayer-funded political advertisements bearing the legend, “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”

The first ad is set to a track by JMSN titled “Love Me” — remember that, it’s important. The ad begins by attacking Marxists, communists and socialists with a voice-over by the president. The second part of the ad lists Trump’s claimed achievements with a voice-over that says, “He is the toughest, most resilient person that I’ve ever met, and nothing was going to stop him from fighting so hard for the country he loves.”

The second ad … well, you should really just watch it for yourself .

If you think this sounds like it could be a campaign ad, that’s because it is. Trump ran the exact same ad back in January 2024.

Normally, I get extremely annoyed with people who try to substitute “common sense” for legal analysis. But even I will admit that you don’t need a law degree to understand why Trump is not allowed to spend the government’s money to run Republican campaign ads.

And there are federal statutes that cover this. For starters, the Consolidated Appropriations Act that currently funds the government forbids government funds from being “used directly or indirectly, including by private contractor, for publicity or propaganda purposes within the United States” unless approved by Congress. Propaganda includes “purely partisan communications” and “self-aggrandizement.”

Trump’s first ad is nothing but self-aggrandizement. (It’s also incredibly cringe worthy, but self-aggrandizement always is.)

The second ad — the one with Trump walking down a hallway — is literally a campaign ad. Communication doesn’t get much more partisan than that. In it, Trump tells us “This is the final battle.” He urges Americans to join him in his fight to “throw off the sick political class that hates our country” and help him “rout the fake news media.”

Trump has already spent $2.5 million of your taxpayer dollars running these ads. Before he’s done, he is planning to spend at least $20 million on them.

His defense is that these are simply public service announcements. “Patriotism isn’t partisan. These public service announcements are unapologetically American, clearly disclosed, and aimed at the country — not a line on the ballot.”

Trump might actually believe this, but that makes it worse, not better. That means Trump thinks that it is unpatriotic to write unflattering things about himself. That’s why he sees no problem with banning critical media outlets from the White House or running ads in praise of himself and about getting rid of “the fake news media.”

Whether it’s tearing down the East Wing, imposing his architectural whims on Washington, or gearing up to interfere with the November election, Trump appears increasingly convinced: “ I am the state .”

I can’t speak for his most loyal voters, but the rest of us have no trouble distinguishing between Trump and America. Nothing is more exuberantly American than a vigorous news media criticizing the government. But a president getting above himself and acting like he’s a French king? Now that’s unpatriotic.

Chris Truax is an appellate attorney who served as Southern California chair for John McCain’s primary campaign in 2008.

articles.title: US jobs market sees sharp slowdown ahead of midterm elections
articles.summary: Unemployment rose slightly as American employers paused hiring with midterm elections just a month away.
articles.body:
The US jobs market saw a sharp slowdown in September, with employers adding just 29,000 jobs in the final update before the midterm elections.

Headcounts were little changed in major sectors from tech to retail as hiring fell significantly from August, according to figures from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).

Meanwhile, the unemployment rate rose slightly from 4.1% in August to 4.2% in September.

The figures signal a cooling US economy, which experts said reduced the likelihood of a series of further interest rate hikes by the Federal Reserve.

The 29,000 jobs created in September was down from a figure of 133,000 in August, according to revised BLS figures for the month.

But George Brown, senior economist at Schroders, said while job gains have been a “rollercoaster“ this year, a single soft report is unlikely to point to a lasting collapse.

And Bradley Saunders, North America economist at Capital Economics, said the lower figure was “not disastrous“, adding that a drop in government roles and temporary visa policy changes weighed on overall growth.

Jeffery Roach, chief economist at LPL Financial, added that the data showed tension between “goods producing sectors that support the AI boom” and service industries feeling the effect of changes brought about by the tech.

“Given the overall softness of the labour market, the likelihood of two Fed hikes is going lower,” he said.

The BLS report stands in sharp contrast to President Donald Trump's insistence that America's economy is booming and it is the "hottest" nation in the world.

The disconnect is likely to present significant challenges as the president and his fellow Republicans hit the the campaign trail with just a month to go before the midterm congressional elections.

According to an AP/NORC poll released on Thursday, just 17% of Americans approve of the president's handling of cost-of-living issues, while 26% approve of his handling of the economy overall.

Both are new lows for Trump, surpassing the lowest mark for Democrat Joe Biden during his presidential term.

There have been some indications that the president understands that his views of the American economy are out of step with those of most Americans.

"I've done a very bad job of explaining how good the country is doing," he said at a White House event earlier this week.

images.caption: Workforces remained unchanged across major sectors, from tech to retail. American firms are choosing to hold steady rather than hire or fire staff

articles.title: Así quedan las votaciones de los dos decretos de la vivienda: el Gobierno no reúne los votos necesarios y no los saca adelante
articles.standfirst: El Congreso de los Diputados ha sometido su aprobación a un pleno extraordinario
articles.summary: El Congreso de los Diputados ha sometido su aprobación a un pleno extraordinario
articles.body: El Congreso de los Diputados ha sometido a votación este viernes 2 de octubre, en un pleno extraordinario, los dos reales decretos ley sobre la vivienda. A grandes rasgos, el primero blinda a los ciudadanos ante los desahucios y el segundo plantea una prórroga obligatoria de los contratos de alquiler. Ambos se han votado por separado. Finalmente, la primera de las votaciones, que ha sido a viva voz, ha obtenido un resultado de 172 votos a favor y 178 votos en contra, así como ninguna abstención. Por lo tanto, el primer decreto de la vivienda no ha salido adelante. De forma inmediata, la votación sobre el segundo decreto también se ha resuelto en el hemiciclo con un resultado idéntico en lo negativo, aunque con 166 votos a favor y 184 votos en contra, siendo tumbado también el segundo paquete de medidas. Las posiciones de la mayoría de las distintas formaciones políticas estaban claras antes del viernes. VOX, PP y UPN avanzaron que votarían en contra de los dos decretos y PSOE y Sumar, obviamente, a favor. Aunque había algunas incógnitas, como Podemos, PNV o Junts, la principal. Ione Belarra ya avanzó que su grupo votaría sí a ambos. Los nacionalistas vascos también despejaron el suspense y confirmaron, ayer por la tarde, que apoyarían el primer decreto, pero no el segundo, el que contemplaba la prórroga de los alquileres. Tras este movimiento, todas las miradas estaban puestas en el partido catalán, que convocó una cumbre telemática ayer por la noche para definir su postura. El segundo decreto, el de la prórroga de los alquileres, era matemáticamente inviable tras el anuncio del voto negativo del PNV. Para que el primero saliera a la luz, Junts debía votar afirmativamente o abstenerse. Existían muchas dudas internas en la formación catalana sobre su papel en el pleno del Congreso. El primer real decreto, publicado el miércoles en el Boletín Oficial del Estado (BOE), incidía, entre otras cuestiones, en frenar los desahucios hasta 2030 y limitar la compra de vivienda por parte de los fondos buitre hasta el 31 de diciembre de 2028. La normativa penaliza fiscalmente las vivienda vacías y carga con más impuestos el alquiler turístico. Además, se anunciaba el mecanismo TU CASA, mediante el que se podría obtener un préstamo a interés cero del 20 por ciento del valor de la vivienda y hasta 50.000 euros (el menor de los dos importes) para la entrada de tu primera vivienda. Como contrapartida, el precio de venta estaría limitado por el Gobierno. El segundo real decreto, publicado en el BOE el jueves, se centra en los contratos de alquiler indefinido, ya que plantea una prórroga obligatoria de cinco años. Si el propietario decide no hacerlo, debería indemnizar al inquilino con doce mensualidades de alquiler de un vivienda de características similares a la que estaría obligado a abandonar.
