articles.body:
America’s former pandemic darling Tony Fauci has crashed back into American politics—dragging several of his former top aides with him, along with the Democrat Party.

This time, the issue is not masks, mandates, lockdowns, or six-foot distancing.

It is a far more fundamental question: Did SARS-CoV-2 emerge from laboratory research in Wuhan involving gain-of-function techniques, and did research funded directly or indirectly through Fauci with American taxpayer dollars help trigger the pandemic?

The Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, chaired by Sen. Rand Paul (R-Ky.), is trying to get answers. Instead, it keeps running into witnesses who invoke their Fifth Amendment right not to testify, lest they incriminate themselves.

First came Fauci himself. Subpoenaed by Paul’s committee, Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment rights 111 times . Then, late last month, another Fauci insider — his special assistant of fifteen years — also took the Fifth .

I had skin in this game from the beginning. As the first Trump administration’s quartermaster during the pandemic, I was working to secure the masks, gloves, gowns, ventilators, testing swabs and other supplies Americans desperately needed. I also helped initiate Operation Warp Speed. And I said publicly on Fox News in April 2020 that the trail of the virus pointed inexorably toward the Wuhan bioweapons lab.

What we desperately lacked at the time was not the published sequence of the virus — that had become available in January, and vaccine scientists rapidly put it to work. What we lacked were the Wuhan laboratory records, virus inventories, raw sequence data, research notebooks, databases and progenitor-virus information that could have told us what had actually happened inside that laboratory.

We were fighting the fog of the pandemic while being denied critical information about its possible source, even as Fauci was engineering his now infamous “Proximal Origin” coverup of the possible lab origins and the possible role of his agency in the creation of the virus.

But Paul now appears to have an unnamed material witness who was standing immediately outside Fauci’s door when the most important conversations occurred.

On January 31, 2020, Wellcome Trust director Jeremy Farrar urgently emailed Fauci asking to speak with him that evening. Fauci’s special assistant, Patricia Conrad, answered on Fauci’s behalf: “Will call shortly.”

What happened next is extraordinary. That same day, scientist Kristian Andersen told Fauci that some features of the virus “(potentially) look engineered.” Fauci has testified that he told Andersen that if the concern held up, the authorities to notify would be the FBI and Britain’s MI5.

But Paul says the committee, reviewing logs Fauci kept on a government computer, found the assistant telling Fauci she had destroyed “a ton of emails” over a weekend — “hundreds, if not thousands” of records, which turns out to have been “a routine practice” in Fauci’s office. Who gave the order? What conversations did she witness? Whom did Fauci call? What happened to those records?

After the assistant invoked the Fifth, Paul offered the obvious mechanism for getting answers: immunity. “It was never our intention really to try to have her indicted,” Paul said . “We wanted to know who gave her the orders.”

Every Republican voted to proceed. Every Democrat voted against. The vote was 8 to 7. Because Paul needed two additional votes for the required two-thirds, the effort failed . Only one Democrat showed up; six voted no by proxy.

Concealment inside Fauci’s agency is no longer hypothetical. David Morens, Fauci’s senior adviser, pleaded guilty in August to conspiracy for hiding federal records on his personal Gmail — records on the EcoHealth gain-of-function grant, its Wuhan subaward, and countering the lab-leak narrative.

This is precisely the territory I explore in my new book “ Why Fauci Must Rot in Prison “ What was happening behind the curtain while decisions affecting hundreds of millions of Americans were being made? And why did Fauci privately text that a second vaccine dose “theoretically could be associated with miscarriage in the first trimester” while publicly telling pregnant women the shots were safe?

Documents tell us what somebody wrote down. Diaries tell us what somebody chose to record. Aides like Morens and Conrad see the machinery.

This should not be a partisan issue. More than a million Americans across party lines died from COVID. Some 17 million adults have have reported long COVID, and more than 11,000 have filed federal claims of injury or death from the vaccines. And all of us were locked down, double-masked, and threatened with firing if we did not submit to the jab.

Yet Democrats have inexplicably circled their wagons around Fauci, who has officially morphed from everybody’s favorite bobblehead into every Democrat’s albatross in November.

Rand Paul is not letting up, and neither am I. Let’s get to the truth.

Peter Navarro is the White House Senior Counselor for Trade and Manufacturing and author of “ Why Fauci Must Rot in Prison .”

articles.title: Christa Pike in critical condition after failed execution attempts: Lawyer
articles.summary: Tennessee inmate Christa Pike was in critical condition and receiving “lifesaving medical care” on Thursday, a day after surviving two failed lethal injection attempts by state executioners, according to her lawyers. Attorney Randy Spivey, who was present at the Wednesday execution attempt, said during a press conference that state executioners “attempted to establish an IV…
articles.body:
Tennessee inmate Christa Pike was in critical condition and receiving “lifesaving medical care” on Thursday, a day after surviving two failed lethal injection attempts by state executioners, according to her lawyers.

Attorney Randy Spivey, who was present at the Wednesday execution attempt, said during a press conference that state executioners “attempted to establish an IV line for an hour” and used seven needles in her left arm alone.

“The state of Tennessee has shown us again that they are not capable of carrying out an execution consistent with basic human dignity,” Spivey said. “Last night was not just inefficient. It was cruel and it was torturous.

“It was also predictable,” he continued, referencing Pike’s lifelong blood disorder that complicated the process of successfully inserting needles into her veins.

“Christa’s legal team told the state of Tennessee and the courts that her medical conditions would cause her to suffer an agonizing death,” the attorney added. “The state and the court dismissed Christa’s concerns.”

Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee (R) ordered that Pike’s execution be delayed until at least next year following the botched attempt to allow for an independent investigation to take place.

This was Tennessee’s second failed execution this year. In May, state executioners failed to locate a vein for a lethal injection for inmate Tony Carruthers. Lee granted a one-year reprieve in the case.

Spivey said the governor’s call for an independent review “does not go far enough” and demanded that Lee immediately commute Pike’s death sentence.

“After having endured solitary confinement for more than 20 years and a full attempt to kill her by lethal injection, Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty,” the lawyer said. “The governor must commute Christa’s sentence now.”

An eleventh-hour stay order from a federal appeals court, which was later lifted by the U.S. Supreme Court, delayed Pike’s scheduled execution time. The high court’s three liberal justices dissented in the decision.

The inmate was convicted of first-degree murder in 1996 after she admitted to killing her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer in Knoxville, Tenn., with Pike’s then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp.

Shipp, who was not eligible for the death penalty since he was 17 at the time of the crime, is serving out a life sentence in prison. His request for parole was denied last year.

May Martinez, the mother of Slemmer, traveled to Nashville to watch the execution. She told The Associated Press she “didn’t get justice” for her daughter after the state’s botched attempt.

“I watched the whole thing. She was awake. She was laughing. She was moving her head, moving her feet. She was trying to sit up,” Martinez said. “Didn’t work the first time they gave her a shot. It didn’t work the second time.”

articles.title: Forget Trump Derangement Syndrome: Trump Fatigue is real, and I’ve got it
articles.summary: Journalist Bernard Goldberg argues that many Americans are experiencing exhaustion from the constant controversies and provocations defining Donald Trump’s second term.
articles.body:
Not that it matters to President Trump, but a lot of Americans are not fans. They don’t like his public vulgarity, his narcissism, his appetite for vengeance and a lot more. But that doesn’t necessarily mean they have Trump Derangement Syndrome, the catch-all diagnosis his supporters like to apply to anyone who finds him objectionable.

They may have another condition brought on by the president. There’s a good chance they’re suffering from Trump Fatigue.

Every day with this president, something new hits the fan. Trump may need a daily dose of chaos, but the rest of us don’t. Chaos and controversy may be his oxygen. They may be what energize him. But after all these years, they’re what wear a lot of us out.

And there’s rarely time to digest one controversy before the next one comes barreling down the road and smacks us in the mouth.

On the first day of his second term, Trump pardoned virtually everyone convicted of crimes related to the Jan. 6, 2021 Capitol riot, while commuting the sentences of several others. His proclamation called the prosecutions a “grave national injustice.”

Since then, in no particular order — because with Donald Trump there really is no particular order — he has made waves saying Canada should become our 51st state.

He threatened to take control of Greenland, refusing at one point to rule out military force.

He never stopped claiming the 2020 presidential election was rigged. Yet at the Republican midterm convention in Dallas last month, he asked supporters to pledge that they would “ cheat like hell ” because, he said, Democrats routinely cheat in elections.

The man who has spent years telling Americans that cheating undermined an election was now standing before supporters, leading them in a pledge … to cheat.

He banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House because he didn’t like what they were saying about him. His administration subsequently defended the bans in court partly on national-security grounds.

He took control of the Kennedy Center’s board which added his name to the building — above that of John F. Kennedy’s name. A federal judge later ruled that the board had exceeded its authority, and Trump’s name was removed.

He demolished the White House East Wing to make way for his great big beautiful golden new ballroom.

And now he wants to build a 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery — what some have dubbed the “Arc de Trump.” When that project ran into legal and preservation challenges, Trump announced that it would also be a “Military Complex/Triumphal Arch,” complete with drones, snipers and ammunition, which he said were necessary for national security.

You couldn’t make this stuff up. And if you did, nobody would buy the screenplay.

Then there are the dopey names he keeps doling out to Democrats — or “Dumocrats,” as he calls them.

James Talarico, the Democratic U.S. Senate candidate in Texas, becomes “James Talafreako.”

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani is “ my little communist .”

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer is “ Cryin’ Chuck Schumer .”

And Democrats generally are now “communists,” with some elevated — or demoted, depending on your point of view — to “ hardcore, godless communists .”

As Joe Biden might put it: “Come on, man.”

Enough already. And that’s the point about Trump Fatigue. It isn’t the same thing as hating Trump. It isn’t even necessarily about disagreeing with his policies. You can support what he’s doing on the border, or taxes, or regulation, or foreign policy and still wonder why every day has to come with another insult, another provocation, another grandiose idea, another enemy, another controversy.

Trump Derangement Syndrome is supposed to describe people who can’t stop thinking about Trump. Trump Fatigue describes people who would occasionally like the opportunity to stop thinking about him.

But Trump makes that almost impossible. He doesn’t merely occupy the presidency. He occupies the national conversation. Morning, noon and night, there he is — demanding attention, picking a fight, settling a score, bestowing a nickname, announcing something nobody saw coming.

And after nearly a decade of this, maybe the remarkable thing isn’t that some Americans are outraged by Donald Trump. Maybe it’s that a lot of us are just plain tired.

Tired of every day being another episode in the longest-running reality show in American political history. Tired of wondering what he said now. Tired of the outrage from one side and the reflexive defense from the other. Tired of a country that seems unable to talk about much of anything without Trump somehow becoming the subject.

Ten minutes after Trump opens his mouth, some of us need a nap. We’re exhausted. And we know one thing for sure: Tomorrow, there’ll be another episode of the Trump show.

That may be good for ratings. But it’s hell on all of us suffering from Trump Fatigue.

Bernard Goldberg is an Emmy and an Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University award-winning writer and journalist. He is the author of five books and publishes exclusive weekly columns, audio commentaries and Q&As on his Substack page .

articles.title: Vance: ‘Really obvious’ Cruz is running for president
articles.summary: Vice President Vance said it was “really obvious” that Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is planning to launch a bid for the White House in 2028 as Vance himself weighs a run as well. “It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president,” Vance said in an interview…
articles.body:
Vice President Vance said it was “really obvious” that Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is planning to launch a bid for the White House in 2028 as Vance himself weighs a run as well.

“It is really obvious to me that, at this very moment, Ted Cruz is running for president,” Vance said in an interview with NBC News. “At this moment, I’m not. I’m trying to help elect Republicans. That’s what I’m going to keep on doing.”

Cruz, who unsuccessfully sought the Republican nomination in 2016, has recently become more open about his interest in the party’s next presidential contest, while Vance has also emerged as a possible contender.

In an interview with MS NOW, Cruz said Vance does not have the 2028 GOP nomination locked down and that he wants to “certainly be part of the discussion.” Cruz also framed the party’s future as a choice between a “small-government, free-market conservative party” and a “big-government, nanny state party.”

A spokesperson for Cruz, who is not up for reelection until 2030, told NBC News that the Texas senator is focused on helping Republicans in this year’s midterm election and will continue campaigning for GOP candidates over the coming weeks.

Vance, meanwhile, has maintained that he will wait until after the midterms before deciding whether to seek the presidency in 2028.

“You make these decisions by collecting as much information and trying to make a wise decision,” Vance said. “And yeah, I mean, regardless of what happens over the next 35 days, there will be new information, new things you have to make a decision over.”

Vance stopped short of saying whether Republican losses would affect whether he runs.

“The American people make that decision, and when they do, then yeah, I’ll have some new information to consider.”

The vice president also said Republicans face an “uphill climb” in the November midterms.

“Historically there’s always a bit of an uphill climb, and I think you definitely sense that,” Vance told NBC News. “I also think you can sense a sense of cautious optimism, in the sense that, you know, people feel like the numbers are sort of moving, maybe in our direction.”

articles.title: Putin won’t likely use nukes, but Kyiv still needs US assistance
articles.summary: There is reason to believe Putin would hesitate to approve a nuclear strike on Ukraine, no matter the situation on the battlefield.
articles.body:
Vladimir Putin has never explicitly said that he would employ nuclear weapons in order to bring the Ukraine war to an end. On the other hand, he has taken several steps to create the impression that Moscow is prepared fire those weapons if it deems it militarily necessary.

These steps include approving an updated nuclear doctrine that appears to lower Russia’s nuclear threshold; stressing Moscow’s readiness to employ nuclear weapons in support of allies such as Ukraine’s neighbor Belarus and moving these weapons onto Belarusian territory; and approving major tactical nuclear drills amidst an uptick in Ukrainian drone attacks.

Moreover, several of Putin’s henchmen have been less coy about their country resorting to tactical nuclear weapons. Most notably, they include former President and current deputy chairman of the Russian National security council Dmitry Medvedev, who has repeatedly threatened their use.

For example, in July 2023, Medvedev responded to a Ukrainian counteroffensive, stating that if “the offensive…succeeded … we would have to use nuclear weapons.” Earlier this year, as the Russian offensive had bogged down while Ukrainian missiles and drones were hitting targets in Moscow, Medvedev asserted that “our patience is not limitless. This ultimate [nuclear option] remains a last resort. … Today we are a few steps from it.”

Both Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese president Xi Jinping have advised the Russian leader against contemplating the use of these weapons. Numerous reports indicate that Modi’s outreach to Putin in 2022 , again two years later, dissuaded the Russian leader from resorting to nuclear weapons. Though neither India nor Russia acknowledged that Modi raised the nuclear issue with Putin, a leading Polish foreign ministry official confirmed in 2025 that three years earlier, Modi had indeed dissuaded Putin from using those weapons.

Xi also appears to have warned Putin on multiple occasions. Like Modi, he did so in 2022 , and he repeated his warning the following year, although in the latter case the Kremlin issued a denial. Interestingly, Moscow has not denied the reports regarding Modi’s outreach to Putin.

In any event, the two leaders’ warnings appear to have fallen upon deaf ears. Current and former Finnish and French military and civilian leaders with whom I met earlier this month have expressed the fear that with the war in Ukraine now in its fifth year and with no end in sight, Putin may indeed be increasingly inclined to carry out Medvedev’s threats.

Moreover, these officials are deeply concerned whether and how the U.S. might respond if Putin actually does order his military to fire one or more nuclear weapons in an attempt to force an end to Ukrainian resistance. They worry that Washington might stand aloof and leave the Ukrainians and their European supporters to their own devices. Somewhat inconsistently, they are equally apprehensive that the U.S. might respond with nuclear weapons of its own, which would then lead to a potentially rapid escalation into a strategic nuclear conflict.

There is nevertheless reason to believe that, whatever his own oblique threats, and the more explicit ones that those like Medvedev have issued, Putin would hesitate to approve a nuclear strike on Ukraine, no matter the situation on the battlefield.

To begin with, the Russian leader is no more certain about an American response than are the Europeans with whom I spoke. He recognizes that a retaliatory strike on Moscow would, at the very minimum, result in the collapse of his regime.

In addition, he faces a second potential nuclear threat from France. France has been a consistent and strong supporter of the Ukrainian cause. At the same time, Paris has been extending its “Forward Nuclear Deterrence Initiative” to an increasing number of European states, which as of mid-September now includes Finland . The French nuclear deterrent is independent of its American counterpart; Putin cannot presume that if Washington holds its nuclear fire, Paris would do the same.

The French have the capability to strike Moscow. My French interlocutors made it clear that Paris would not rule out the possibility of a retaliatory strike.

With two independent sources of uncertainty as to how the West might respond to a Russian nuclear strike, Putin is unlikely to order one, even in the most extreme case. Instead, Russia will likely to continue to intensify missile and drone attacks on Ukrainian civilian as well as military infrastructure.

Putin may not resort to a nuclear option, but with Moscow increasingly employing jet-powered drones and missiles to attack Ukrainian targets at all hours, Kyiv has an urgent and dire need for additional defensive assets. Western Europe continues to provide some support in this regard, but even with its munitions running low, America nevertheless should make every effort to provide additional assistance to Kyiv’s ongoing battle to preserve its freedom and independence.

Dov S. Zakheim is a senior adviser at the Center for Strategic and International Studies and vice chairman of the board for the Foreign Policy Research Institute. He was undersecretary of Defense (comptroller) and chief financial officer for the Department of Defense from 2001 to 2004 and a deputy undersecretary of Defense from 1985 to 1987 .

articles.title: Slovenia's .si domain sees a surge in registrations after Trump's 'super intelligence' order | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The .si domain name is seeing unprecedented demand after President Trump's super intelligence executive order.
articles.body:
In not-so-surprising news, the .si domain name is seeing unprecedented demand after President Trump signed an executive order mandating all government agencies to refer to “AI” and “artificial intelligence” as “SI” and “super intelligence.” It echoes what happened at the start of the AI boom, when interest in the .ai domain name — associated with the country Anguilla — spiked and brought in millions for the island territory.

Now it’s .si’s turn in the spotlight. The domain name was commonly associated with Slovenia, where, ironically, First Lady Melania Trump is from. Klara Herman, a spokesperson at Registry SI, the official organization that manages Slovenia’s domains, told the BBC earlier this week that there was a 2,199% increase in .si domain name purchases in September. However, she was cautious about linking the boost only to President Trump.

Still, the Registry noted 11,000 new addresses recorded on September 30, the day after President Trump signed the executive order , and almost 13,000 new .si domain names were registered in the past 24 hours.

We reached out to a few other web hosting sites to see if they had seen similar trends. GoDaddy said they don’t yet host the .si domain, and Squarespace hadn’t yet responded as of the time of publication. Wix, interestingly enough, said that they weren’t seeing any “meaningful uptick” on their end, and that it’s been minimal on the site since September 29. “It’s still early so that could change,” a Wix spokesperson said.

But web hosting platform Hostinger told me that .si is now its second most popular domain extension, right after .com. It found that among its customers, almost 4,300 registered .si on September 30 and about 5,400 on October 1; more than three-quarters of all .si domains registered since September 23 came in the last two days. It found that more than half the buyers were coming from the U.S. and India.

Curiously enough, on Hostinger, only around 3% of the .si domains are explicitly related to AI, it said. Most are “unclassified” — meaning their names don’t match any specific category. It said that most of those registering the .si domain name seem to be people and businesses, though there is a speculative element, in that people could be buying the domains to resell them later.

Upon hearing this, my first thought went back to what a founder messaged me earlier this week, noting that .si domains were reselling for over a million dollars. Kim Than, CEO of Genius PR, who specializes in working with AI and crypto founders, told me that he already bought the .si version of his company name “to protect the brand in case this takes off like .ai.” And did so because it was cheap, so he figured he might as well “secure it now than potentially pay a lot more later.”

Than sees domain names as digital collectibles and wants to pick up a few more while the price is still good, and he might resell them later; one can also tokenize domains, he said, and trade them on the blockchain, though he’s not sure if .si is supported just yet. “A few founder friends are buying too ’cause we think it’s the new AI boom,” he continued. “Who knows how far it goes, but I’m happy to take a bet.”

There is a chance that .si could become pretty popular. President Trump’s executive order said that “the capabilities of today’s frontier systems do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence,” and that they “increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence but a new super intelligence.”

Klaudijus Januitis, head of domains at Hostinger, told me that he expects the demand for .si to keep growing, though he doesn’t see that domain replacing .ai anytime soon. Instead, as noted by that founder and his friends, Januitis said .si is right now a more available and a “more affordable second option.”

“Slovenia will not see what Anguilla saw,” he said, noting that, for one, Anguilla charges a “premium” to use .ai and that money goes straight to the government, while .si is a fraction of the cost and goes to the registry rather than the treasury. For example, on Hostinger, .si costs around $12 dollars a year while .ai goes for $90 and requires a two-year commitment. “For Anguilla, .ai became a second economy. For Slovenia, .si is a nice bonus.”

articles.title: GOP senator says midterms could be like 2006: ‘And 2006 was really bad for Republicans’
articles.summary: Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) is warning that Republicans could get drubbed in this year’s midterm election, much like what happened to Republicans 20 years ago during former President George W. Bush’s second midterm elections, when the GOP lost control of both the House and Senate. Daines, who headed the Senate Republican campaign arm in the…
articles.body:
Sen. Steve Daines (R-Mont.) is warning that Republicans could get drubbed in this year’s midterm election, much like what happened to Republicans 20 years ago during former President George W. Bush’s second midterm elections, when the GOP lost control of both the House and Senate.

Daines, who headed the Senate Republican campaign arm in the last election cycle, says there are alarming similarities between the 2026 and 2006 elections that don’t bode well for GOP candidates, such as the nation being mired in an unpopular war and high gas prices.

“There arguably could be some similarities between the ’06 cycle and the 2026 cycle. Think about the condition of the country back in ’06. An unpopular war, 6 in 10 Americans opposed the Iraq War at that point. Gas prices had doubled. Does it sound familiar? We ended up losing six seats,” Daines said at the Grand Strategy Summit in Washington.

“That was a night, by the way, we lost some redder states,” he added.

Republicans held a five-seat majority in the Senate at the start of the 2006 election cycle, and most political handicappers projected they would keep their majority at the start of the cycle, but they wound up losing six seats because of voter anger over the war in Iraq, high gas prices and scandals in Washington.

GOP senators lost in several Republican-leaning states that year, including Sen. Mike DeWine (R), who lost to Democrat Sherrod Brown in Ohio; Sen. Conrad Burns (R), who lost to Democrat Jon Tester in Montana; and Sen. Jim Talent (R) who lost to Democrat Claire McCaskill in Missouri.

“Today 6 in 10 Americans oppose the Iran war. Gas prices — enough said on gas prices. There’s an argument, if you look at history, that 2026 feels a lot like 2006,” Daines said.

Democrats picked up 32 seats in the House in 2006, giving the Speaker’s gavel to Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.).

Former Sen. Harry Reid (D-Nev.) became the Senate majority leader in 2007.

President Trump acknowledged on Thursday that “it’s possible” that the Iran war could cost Republicans seats in Congress this November.

Trump registered only a 26 percent job approval rating in an Associated Press/NORC Center for Public Affairs poll of 2,140 U.S. adults conducted from Sept. 24 to 28.

The survey showed that 69 percent of Americans think the war with Iran has not been worth fighting, and only 28 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s handling of the conflict.

Decision Desk HQ gives Democrats a 75 percent chance of winning the House in November and a 54 percent chance of winning the Senate.

articles.title: DOJ moves to boot federal judges from immigration cases over NYT interview
articles.summary: The Justice Department filed a judicial misconduct complaint against seven Minnesota federal judges over a New York Times immigration interview.
articles.body: The Justice Department wants several Minnesota federal judges removed from immigration cases after accusing them of crossing an ethical line by publicly criticizing President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown. The complaint argued the judges improperly commented on the Trump administration's immigration enforcement while related cases were still pending, undermining public confidence in their impartiality. Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Wednesday that the Justice Department filed a judicial misconduct complaint with the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals against seven Minnesota federal judges over their participation in a New York Times interview published last September. "These judges talked to the media, or at least The New York Times, about cases, some of which are ongoing, in a manner which the Department views as a clear violation of their ethical duties," Blanche said. ‘UNPRECEDENTED’: JUDGES REVEAL BEHIND-THE-SCENES COORDINATION ON TRUMP IMMIGRATION CASES The complaint specifically names Judge Patrick Schiltz, appointed by President George W. Bush, and Judge John Tunheim, a Clinton appointee, along with unnamed district judges who also participated in the interviews. The Justice Department asked the Eighth Circuit's Judicial Council to investigate the judges' conduct and order Schiltz and Tunheim to recuse themselves from Department of Homeland Security immigration cases, arguing that their impartiality could reasonably be questioned. But, whether that happens, however, is not up to the Justice Department. Under the federal judiciary's judicial misconduct process, complaints are reviewed within the judicial branch. The chief judge of the circuit — which for the Eighth Circuit is Steven Colloton, a Bush-appointee — would first determine whether a complaint should be dismissed or referred to a special committee for further investigation, according to the Administrative Office of the U.S. Courts. If a committee is appointed, it submits findings to the circuit's Judicial Council, which decides whether any corrective action is appropriate. The judiciary also notes that the misconduct process "cannot be used to obtain automatic disqualification of a judge presiding over a case" or simply challenge a judge's legal rulings. OBAMA, BIDEN JUDGES DRAW FRESH FIRE AS TRUMP’S IMMIGRATION COURT CLASHES HEAT UP: ‘ALMOST IMPOSSIBLE’ The Justice Department's complaint stemmed from a Sept. 17, 2026, New York Times article in which Judge Schiltz and Tunheim and six other Minnesota federal judges discussed the wave of immigration litigation that followed the Trump administration's "Operation Metro Surge." The judges described an unprecedented influx of habeas petitions and reflected on how the cases strained court resources, while also expressing concerns about aspects of the administration's immigration enforcement efforts. Both Schiltz, who sat for a nearly 90-minute interview, and Tunheim made remarks that were specifically cited in the DOJ complaint. BLANCHE TORCHES TRUMP FOE BOASBERG AFTER APPEALS COURT BLOCKS JUDGE AGAIN IN DEPORTATION FIGHT The Department argued those interviews crossed an ethical line because they addressed issues involved in active litigation. The complaint cited comments attributed to Schiltz describing the administration's actions as threatening "the constitutional order" and "the rule of law," as well as remarks from Tunheim criticizing the administration's immigration arrests. The Justice Department alleged that those statements violated the Code of Conduct for United States Judges by commenting publicly on ongoing matters and creating the appearance that the judges had prejudged issues that were likely to come before them. "The Framers insulated judges so they would exercise judgment, not will," Chad Mizelle, chair of Litigation for America First Policy Institute, wrote on X. "What we have now is the inverse: a bench enslaved to its own political ideology. When judges become politicians in a robe, the system starts to collapse." Mizelle pointed out that, in the past, judges have been removed from cases due to their conversations with the press, which "created an appearance of bias." "In 2001, Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson gave embargoed interviews, including to the Times, while handling United States v. Microsoft," Mizelle wrote on X. "The D.C. Circuit called that conduct 'deliberate, repeated, egregious and flagrant' and removed him from the case. That standard still applies. What has changed is the willingness of sitting judges to ignore it." Meanwhile Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison chalked the complaint up to be the Trump administration's attempt to intimidate judges. "This complaint has nothing to do with judicial ethics and everything to do with political punishment," Ellison said in a statement. "Blanche and Trump are trying to punish the judges who ruled against federal government actions during Operation Metro Surge — including the Administration’s undisputed non-compliance at the time with hundreds of court orders — even though sometimes the court ruled with the government."

articles.title: My drones save lives — but the FCC wants to take them away
articles.summary: Drones have been a game-changer for my team at Weber County Search and Rescue here in Utah, but unfortunately, a proposal under consideration in Washington, D.C., could cut off our ability to buy them, and hurt search and rescue teams like mine all across the country.
articles.body:
When someone is lost in the wilderness, time is of the essence. A few minutes can mean the difference between life and death for a hiker who wanders off the trail or a snowmobiler who doesn’t make it back — particularly at night, when temperatures plummet.

Drones have been a game-changer for my team at Weber County Search and Rescue here in Utah, but unfortunately, a proposal under consideration in Washington, could cut off our ability to buy them, and hurt search and rescue teams like mine all across the country.

Here in the mountains, drones have fundamentally transformed the way we conduct rescues. We save more lives and get rescuers back home to their families faster and safer than ever before, thanks to this new technology.

Two years ago, a snowboarder went missing in North Fork, off the trail, after dark. As ice started to form on his skin, our team launched a drone with a thermal camera. We had eyes on him in just 10 minutes, compared to the hours it would have taken ground teams searching in the dark or to get a helicopter up in the air.

I estimate that my team alone has saved between 25 and 30 lives in situations just like this, and we have cut our average search time from four and a half hours to less than one hour. We have also been able to do it with limited resources. A helicopter can cost millions of dollars — and that’s just to buy the aircraft, not even factoring in the cost for crew, fuel or having it ready to go when an emergency arises. We were able to purchase our whole fleet of 12 drones for roughly $90,000, a fraction of the cost, and well worth it for the lifesaving air capability they provide.

Yet recently, the Federal Communications Commission put forward a proposal that would categorize most of the drones we use as “military-grade” equipment, including the thermal drone that saved that snowboarder’s life. Their reasoning is that capabilities such as the thermal imaging essential in missing persons searches and LiDAR, which helps the drone avoid obstacles such as trees and cliff faces, somehow means the drone should not be available to everyday Americans for purchase.

I don’t pretend to be a policy expert, but I do know what my drones can do, and I know the difference between what works in a high-stakes rescue situation and what doesn’t. Unfortunately, the American-made drones on the market just aren’t there yet. They cost three to eight times as much and deliver less than half the capacity of our models, including shorter flight times, weaker thermal sensors and less reliable performance in inclement weather conditions, such as high winds or cold temperatures. I have tested them, and none have been able to match what my team’s current fleet can do.

Of course I want to support a strong American drone industry. We all should. But if this proposal goes through, foreign manufacturers aren’t the ones hurt most. It’s the small counties and volunteer teams that cannot absorb a massive price hike on life-saving equipment, or cannot trust drones that don’t deliver when lives are on the line. Already, we have been pressured by restrictions on drones in recent years, and this latest proposal out of the FCC goes even further by targeting the exact tools that search and rescue teams need most.

We aren’t alone in our concerns, either — an analysis by the Pilot Institute found that 98.6 percent of comments opposed the proposal, with just 16 comments in support. A significant number of these are from agencies just like mine.

I invite any policymaker in Washington who is skeptical of how stark the difference is to come visit us in Utah and see for yourself how these drones save lives. See how we fly these missions, see what we can spot with the drones that would be invisible to rescue teams on the ground, and see how quickly we can do it. See side-by-side how the American drones match up to the equipment you want to ban.

Once you do, you will ask yourself what equipment you would want the rescue team to have if it was your own family lost in the mountains — and why anyone would want to take these drones out of our hands when they are the best chance we have to get people home safely.

Kyle Nordfors is the sUAS Team Coordinator for Weber County Search and Rescue in Northern Utah and the UAS Chairman for the Mountain Rescue Association, covering more than 90 Search and Rescue teams in North America. A 25-year aviation veteran, he is also a current Boeing 737 Captain for one of America’s legacy airlines.

articles.title: Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87
articles.summary: The defeat raises pressure on Sánchez to call a snap election, after a series of scandals affecting his party and allies.
articles.body:
Spain's Congress has rejected a series of measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis, in a defeat for the government of Pedro Sánchez that increases pressure on him to call a snap election.

Lawmakers voted on two decree-laws presented by the government in response to nationwide protests that have followed the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, from her home.

The decrees, which introduced a series of initiatives aimed at protecting tenants in the rental market, required parliamentary approval in order to remain in place.

MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.

Hundreds of demonstrators had gathered outside Congress as the debate took place and there were angry scenes.

Protesters chanted "shame on you" and "your profits, our misery", after the results were announced.

The government's defeat underlines the fact that Sánchez, a Socialist, does not command a congressional majority and it has heightened speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.

Sources told Spanish media that the government would spend the weekend deciding its next step, and whether to dissolve parliament.

Sánchez's beleaguered government had already been mired in a series of scandals and judicial cases affecting his Socialist Party and close allies.

Abascal was evicted after she was unable to pay a sharp rent increase introduced by Urbagestión, the company that owned her flat in central Madrid.

Hundreds of protesters gathered to oppose the eviction last week and the case triggered a broader movement across the country demanding affordable rentals, which have soared in recent years.

The social backlash has seen Urbagestión negotiate the return of Abascal to her flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued, with people occupying squares in Madrid and other cities, pitching tents in squares and with a series of marches scheduled for this weekend.

The Sindicato de Inquilinas (Tenants' Union) activist association which has been co-ordinating protests, announced during the congressional debate that it was abandoning the tent protest in central Madrid. It said it wanted to "take the struggle to all the neighbourhoods, residential blocks and homes of Madrid, wherever there are rental increases, expulsions and abuses each day, and turn the energy of the last few days into a permanent organisation".

Protesters are also calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.

The left-wing coalition government responded to the social anger by hurriedly drawing up the two decree-laws in an effort to defuse the protests.

The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".

The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Sindicato de Inquilinas .

The conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.

However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.

Friday's debate was fierce and at times angry, as supporters and opponents of the decrees clashed in Congress.

"I don't ask you, I beg you to be brave and consistent," Sánchez said, moments before the two votes took place. "Because they are not just ambitious measures, they are necessary".

He appealed to lawmakers "to put order and humanity into [the housing] market, because if we don't, it will bring down our society".

Social Affairs minister Pablo Bustinduy, of the Sumar alliance, the junior partner in the governing coalition, presented the debate in dramatic terms.

"Today is about defending an international oligarchy which is extracting the rent from salaries earned with the effort of working classes of this country in order to share it out with dividends and they don't even pay taxes in Spain," he said.

"Voting against these decrees today means defending the interests of this oligarchy and turning your back on your own people."

However, Miriam Nogueras, of JxCat, said the decrees had been hastily drawn up and lacked rigour.

She said the decrees "will allow [vulture] funds to keep buying, keep speculating and evictions to keep happening… these two decrees would provoke the opposite effect of what they aim to achieve."

The political right has argued that the government's attempts to intervene will frighten homeowners, causing them not to put their properties on the rental market and pushing prices up further.

Juan Bravo of the PP said "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".

articles.title: Trump campaign insider reveals strategy behind midterm blitz that White House hopes pays off big
articles.summary: Donald Trump's 32-state rally tour through deep red states has a hidden strategy that pundits are missing, says a veteran campaign strategist.
articles.body: A veteran campaign strategist who worked for Donald Trump's 2024 reelection bid told Fox News Digital that pundits are misreading the strategy behind the president's 32-state pre-midterms rally tour, which includes stops in deep red states. Thursday, the president spoke in Denton, Texas, a suburb of Dallas before traveling to Oklahoma, a longtime bastion of conservatism that hasn't been carried by a Democrat in a presidential election since Lyndon B. Johnson in 1964. Trump on Friday will rally in Mobile, Alabama, another traditionally Republican-dominated state. While political analysts speculate Trump's blitz signals doom for the GOP in November, Luke Ball, who knows intimately the inner-workings of how the 47th president operates on the campaign trail, has a different view. CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN? GOP BETS ON TRUMP AT HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION "So for people who are maybe commenting and doing it from a perspective of ‘the president's in trouble,’ I think that’s kind of a lazy analysis for you to just take it at surface value that he’s in red states," Ball said. He added that Texas and Oklahoma go "hand in hand," and that the appearing in both places can boost Republican midterm turnout in November across swing district or more competitive districts found in some deep red states. Though he admits the strategy is a "risk" for Trump, he says the month-long tour isn't a fly-by-night operation. GOP FACES BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS REPUBLICANS PAINT ELECTION AS ‘COMPETITION WITH COMMUNISM’ "They keep saying — and it's a risk politically for the president — but they keep saying that he is on the ballot and on the top of the ballot, but the reason they're doing it is because the RNC the MAGA Incs, and the James Blair's of the world have the data that show who's going to turn out for the president and nobody else," said Ball. MAGA Inc. is a Super PAC that poured more than $375 million into electing Trump in 2024, and is now backing Republican congressional candidates nationwide. James Blair was Trump's 2024 campaign political director, and is now the White House Deputy Chief of Staff. BLACK CONSERVATIVE REVEALS HOW GOP CAN LOCK DOWN MINORITY VOTERS WITHOUT TRUMP ON BALLOT "The next stop is in Mobile, Alabama, another media market that I worked in, which is going to encompass Pensacola, Florida — which always brings out the vote for the rest of the state," Ball said. "So if you want to solidify your standing in Florida and show that you still are the kingmaker in that state that used to be purple a few years ago, and now Democrats don't even bother spending in it, you've got to make sure that you lock that down." "So, great optics in Alabama, great optics in Oklahoma, but in addition to that, you're getting a red area of Texas motivated to turn out and a very, very red area of Florida to turn out for those elections." It's also from a perspective too, when you have these major rallies in Mobile, Alabama, or Oklahoma or deep red states across the nation, that still gets major national coverage." articles.title: If America wants to prosper, we must lead
articles.summary: Sen. Rick Scott and Hudson Institute Fellow Rebeccah Heinrichs argue that the United States must maintain global leadership to counter an emerging authoritarian alliance led by China and Russia.
articles.body:
Last week at the United Nations General Assembly , President Trump issued a “challenge for every nation in this room” to “go forward strong and united against the enemies of all humanity” and, by doing so, “make this world a far better and safer place.” While it is tempting to write Trump’s words off as rhetorical fanfare, the mission they describe is real, critical and — unfortunately — now being dismissed by many in the U.S.

Lately, a foolish worldview is growing in popularity among elected leaders in Washington. You hear it from voices ranging from Tucker Carlson to Hasan Piker. Some on the left and right have become convinced that solving America’s domestic issues requires our retreat from leadership on the world stage.

Their narrative requires us to ignore history and believe that America is in irreversible decline and has shriveled in form from her former greatness. But America’s best days are ahead, and we can and must stay energetically engaged in foreign policy to protect Americans and our way of life. And so, we must be clear about what a U.S. retreat would mean and how American life would look if we allowed Communist China to write the rules and our enemies to establish a New World Order.

These views, often sold as populist ideas, are nothing new. Nearly a century ago, America faced similar choices as evil around the world began to threaten our security.

In the fall of 1939, the devastation caused by the Great Depression hung like a dark cloud over the lives of many Americans while Nazi Germany invaded Poland. While the news out of Europe was troubling, there were plenty of “leaders” in Washington telling hardworking families that America couldn’t possibly be worried about the security of Europe when our own citizens couldn’t guarantee the security of their own jobs.

These are the same arguments being sold today as young Americans worry about grocery bills, the cost of electricity, and how they are going to afford to raise a family. Of course, the choice between global leadership and domestic prosperity is a false one.

The American Dream depends on the United States’ leadership in the world, where we set rules in a way that protects the American people, secures our economy, and advances our goals.

America First is not possible if America surrenders its position on the world stage. We want an America strong enough to deter our enemies and win a war if an adversary starts one. That does not mean getting entangled in forever wars and needless regime change operations with no goal and no endgame.

What the Tucker-Piker camp fails to understand is that America still has enemies. Communist China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and Cuba have created an anti-American coalition — an authoritarian alliance — to undercut us as the global superpower and sever the ties between the U.S. and the Western coalition.

And it doesn’t end with China — Russia is waging a war of choice in Ukraine to test the resolve of NATO and to scare Americans into believing that they must surrender peace among their oldest and most prosperous Western democracies or risk catastrophic war.

Those powers — supported by authoritarians in Iran, North Korea and Cuba — are consolidating with one goal: undermine the United States, replace its influence with those of authoritarian powers, and undermine the world that the West has built.

This is happening at different levels and with different methods. The Chinese Communist Party is leveraging economic dependence against the West to bend our allies toward its interests. Russia is attempting to break NATO to claim territory from sovereign democratic nations. Iran is destabilizing the Middle East and global trade. Meanwhile, North Korea is investing in its illegal nuclear missile program while providing soldiers to Russia for its war against Ukraine .

All four nations are collaborating in various ways, and aim to push the U.S., its forward deployed bases, and its influence out of their regions. In our own, Cuba has proven to be the greatest destabilizing force in the Western Hemisphere for decades.

I have no doubt our foreign adversaries see a useful domestic asset in Islamist-Socialist Hasan Piker — an American via birthright citizenship only — who wants capitalists dead , believed 9/11 was justified , and campaigns for socialists in our elections.

It cannot be any clearer: the authoritarian alliance desires the destruction of the postwar order, and the rights and prosperity generations have died defending.

If we retreat and allow this authoritarian alliance to take hold, America will suffer. Communist China and its accomplices will starve us, isolate us, and deprive us of every resource possible until America is weak and dependent. We will have no autonomy, no opportunity, and no freedom. Our financial markets will be powerless to fuel innovation, our business will shutter, and the American Dream will die.

President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio understand what’s at stake, and they’ve shown that there’s a smarter way to do it than the mistakes we’ve seen this century. They showed the world America is not giving up. President Trump made NATO allies recommit to the alliance and have encouraged others outside the alliance to join the cause.

They also understand the need to reduce our exposure to our enemies, especially via trade. Every dollar we send to Beijing — and the rest of the authoritarian alliance — is capital for them to hurt us and our allies.

Retreating from the challenges to our power will not appease them; it only increases the cost of confronting them down the road. Strong leadership creates the environment for domestic security and economic prosperity. Without it, America and her allies remain vulnerable to criminal regimes who hate our way of life.

We cannot sacrifice national and global security to a false dilemma of domestic versus overseas issues. It is not a zero-sum equation. To believe it would destroy a century of American greatness and the American Dream itself.

Americans deserve a future that is safe, prosperous and free. For that to happen, America must lead.

Rick Scott is Florida’s senior U.S. senator. He serves on the Foreign Relations and Armed Services committees. Rebeccah Heinrichs is a senior fellow at Hudson Institute and the director of its Keystone Defense Initiative.

articles.title: Talarico leads Paxton by 2 points in tightening Texas Senate race: Survey
articles.summary: Texas state Rep. James Talarico (D) is leading state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) by just 2 points among likely voters, according to a new Fox News poll. The Democrat’s lead is within the poll’s 3-point margin of error and shows a tight race in the Lone Star State. Among likely voters polled, 51 percent…
articles.body:
Texas state Rep. James Talarico (D) is leading state Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) by just 2 points among likely voters, according to a new Fox News poll .

The Democrat’s lead is within the poll’s 3-point margin of error and shows a tight race in the Lone Star State. Among likely voters polled, 51 percent said they support Talarico while 49 percent sided with Paxton.

The Texas Senate race is important to both parties’ efforts to control the upper chamber, with Democrats attempting to win a state-wide race in Texas for the first time in decades. The poll shows 49 percent of likely voters said they would prefer a Democratic-controlled Senate, while 50 percent favored Republicans.

“Democrats in Texas will walk across broken glass to vote against [President] Trump, so the question is whether the average Republican will vote in an election without Trump and where the Senate race features a controversial GOP candidate,” pollster Daron Shaw said in the poll’s online release.

Talarico has garnered solid support from Black voters at 79 percent, moderate voters at 65 percent and Hispanic voters at 64 percent. Paxton’s key demographic support comes from White evangelical Christians, 74 percent, white men without a college degree at 65 percent, rural voters at 57 percent and voters over the age of 65 at 55 percent.

There’s an even wider gap in likely voters’ favorability ratings of the two candidates, with Talarico earning an 8-point net positive rating while Paxton comes in at 18 points underwater.

The poll found Republicans are more than six times more likely to hold an unfavorable view of Paxton than Democrats do of Talarico.

While the race is narrow among likely voters, Talarico holds a wider 7-point lead — outside the margin of error — among the larger pool of registered voters. The poll also found more MAGA Republicans are extremely interested in the election compared with non-MAGA Republicans, while voters identified with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) are nearly equally as likely to be interested in the midterms as their non-DSA counterparts.

Seventy percent of likely voters reported that the cost of living will be important to their Senate vote, with Talarico leading Paxton by 32 points among those who said they are falling behind economically. Respondents who said they are getting ahead economically support Paxton by a 48-point advantage, and those who said they are holding steady economically backed Paxton by 3 points.

A majority of likely voters said Talarico was too liberal, 53 percent, and that Paxton was too close to Trump, 51 percent. Nearly half of respondents said Trump will be extremely important to their vote.

Fox News also polled the race for Texas governor between incumbent Greg Abbott (R) and state Rep. Gina Hinojosa (D). Abbott leads Hinojosa 52 percent to 47 percent with a 52 percent approval rating for the sitting governor. The poll found 10 percent of Talarico supporters are backing Abbott for reelection.

“Ironically, Paxton may owe his political life to Abbott, who is doing most of the get-out-the-vote work for the Republicans,” Shaw said.

The poll surveyed 1,203 randomly selected registered voters fielded through phone-call interviews or online surveys sent by text message Sept. 24-28. The poll surveyed likely voters and registered voters with margins of error of 3 points and 2.5 points, respectively.

articles.title: Trump is expected to name intelligence director Jay Clayton as AI czar
articles.summary: President Trump is expected to name Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the White House AI czar, according to a source familiar with the matter.
articles.body: President Trump is expected to name Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the White House’s artificial intelligence czar, according to a source familiar with the matter. The president teased the move this week and will most likely announce it on social media as early as Friday, the source said. It comes after a lengthy meeting with executives of leading technology companies at the White House on Tuesday, which Clayton attended. Clayton, who oversees the nation’s spy agencies as the director of national intelligence, would take on the AI responsibility alongside his current role. When reached for a comment about the forthcoming announcement, a White House official said, “Any personnel announcement will be announced directly by the President. Any reporting until then is baseless speculation.” In a CNBC interview Wednesday the White House AI meeting, Clayton said the Trump administration would be taking a “whole-of-government approach” to regulating the technology. “Superintelligence is a national security issue,” Clayton said, using the term the Trump administration has formally adopted to refer to AI. “That was something that was recognized yesterday by not just the industry leaders, but everybody in the room.” David Sacks, who now serves as co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, had served as special adviser for AI and Crypto from January 2025 through March of this year. Trump’s selection of Clayton comes after a groundswell of concern about the consequences associated with AI development following warnings by employees at some of the top AI companies about the technology putting humanity at risk. Trump has largely brushed off these threats, including after his meeting with AI giants, pushing back on calls to implement stronger safety regulations. “I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing, and they understand that they have to self-police, and it’s very hard for somebody to come outside, get into these. These models are very complex, and again, I believe they’re going to be used for the good,” Trump told reporters at the White House. “And when they’re not, we’re going to be able to nab them. But there’s going to be a tremendous self-policing aspect.” Before he took over the DNI role in August following Senate confirmation, Clayton was the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York. He was chair of the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term and previously a partner at top law firm Sullivan & Cromwell.

articles.title: Republican super PAC shifts money from North Carolina to Kansas
articles.summary: The Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), a Republican PAC that raises money and spends on ads supporting GOP Senate candidates, is moving money out of North Carolina and into Kansas, according to a source familiar with SLF’s plans. The move is a sign that the Kansas race is growing more competitive for Democrats, as polls suggest…
articles.body:
The Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), a Republican PAC that raises money and spends on ads supporting GOP Senate candidates, is moving money out of North Carolina and into Kansas, according to a source familiar with SLF’s plans.

The move is a sign that the Kansas race is growing more competitive for Democrats, as polls suggest the GOP’s chances of winning in North Carolina are narrowing.

The PAC is pausing its $30 million advertising campaign in support of Michael Whatley, former Republican National Committee chair, in North Carolina amid his tight race with Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper.

Cooper is favored to win , according to elections analysts, and one recent poll had him 11 points ahead.

The change was first reported by Semafor .

North Carolina is still not a slam dunk, however. SLF still has $15 million reserved for the state throughout the fall and President Trump stumped for Whatley in Charlotte in September.

“A Democrat has not won statewide federal office here in nearly two decades, and North Carolina is a 50-50 state,” said Jeff Allen, campaign manager for Cooper. “We’re building a campaign to earn every vote and make sure North Carolinians know that Roy Cooper will fight for them, while Michael Whatley will continue to enrich himself at their expense.

The race in Kansas, usually a safe Republican seat in the Senate, has tightened in recent weeks as Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton, founding pastor of one of the state’s largest churches, emerged from the primary field and has garnered attention and money, while taking aim at incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall’s (R) support for the unpopular Iran war and other Trump administration policies.

Elections analysts shifted that race slightly more in Democrats’ favor last month, though Marshall is still seen as the favorite.

According to AdImpact, a website that tracks advertising spending in politics, the SLF has reserved $485,000 so far for the Kansas Senate race, and ads are set to begin next week. One ad against Hamilton, released Friday morning , calls him a “two-faced extremist,” pushing against Hamilton’s narrative that he is politically moderate.

The SLF has also recently put more money into Midwest states like Iowa and Ohio , which were once expected to be safer for Republican candidates but now face similar challenges as Kansas.

articles.title: $2.5 billion Amazon settlement: More payments being sent out, with another round possible
articles.summary: More people now qualify for the massive settlement, which may produce another round of automatic payments next year.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – More — and larger — payments connected to a $2.5 billion settlement Amazon reached with the Federal Trade Commission last year may soon be available, according to officials.

The settlement came last year after Amazon was accused of using “deceptive methods” to register millions of customers for paid Prime subscriptions, then making it difficult for those customers to cancel. Amazon did not admit wrongdoing .

Of the $2.5 billion involved in the settlement, $1.5 billion was to be used on customer refunds .

Some impacted consumers received automatic payments late last year as part of the agreement. Another group had to complete a claims process . At the time, the FTC said payments were capped at $51, but could be less than $1 .

Now, following a joint motion from the FTC and Amazon, “millions” more are now eligible for automatic payouts, and another round of payments may be sent out.

More consumers now qualify for payment, FTC says

Part of the original qualifications was that you had to have used fewer than 10 Prime benefits during a one-year period after becoming a member. Now, the FTC says automatic payments will be provided to “millions of additional consumers who used between 11 and 20 Prime benefits during a one-year period.”

You still need to have either signed up for Prime with Amazon’s “challenged enrollment flow” (including signing up through the universal Prime decision page, shipping selection page, single page checkout, or the Prime Video enrollment flow) or tried but failed to cancel your U.S. subscription. Either needs to have happened between June 23, 2019, and June 23, 2025.

Amazon was expected to start sending funds via Venmo, PayPal, or a check in the mail to members of this group on Thursday.

Additionally, if you were notified that you qualified for this settlement, but did not file a claim before the July deadline, you may instead receive an automatic payment from Amazon if you are deemed eligible.

As part of the joint motion, the payment cap may adjust from $51 to $200. That means those who received a $51 payment may see another totaling up to $149.

You do not need to do anything to receive this second round of payments, according to settlement administrators .

It’s not yet clear whether these additional payments will actually be sent out, though. It will come down to whether the “consumer-accepted payments … reach the required threshold by February 2027,” according to the FTC . As of September, Amazon had distributed more than $845 million, but less than the $1.5 billion it was required to pay in redress.

You have 30 days to accept a digital payment to receive the funds, or 60 days to cash a check, if you opt for that method. You can find more details on the settlement website , including instructions on what to do if you are unable to redeem your payment.

Should another round of payments happen, the FTC said it will start by April 2027 and distribution will happen automatically.

articles.title: Trump to name intelligence chief Jay Clayton as AI tsar: Reports
articles.summary: The possible selection comes amid increasing calls for the government to intervene in the rapidly developing technology.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump is expected to select spy chief Jay Clayton to oversee development of the nation’s artificial intelligence industry, according to multiple news reports.

CNN, CBS and Axios reported Trump is set to name the director of national intelligence (DNI) as his pick for so-called “AI tsar”. The decision could be announced as early as Friday.

Amid increasing calls for the government to intervene in the rapidly developing technology, Trump last month announced on social media that he would be naming a new AI tsar. “Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” he wrote.

Trump already had one AI tsar, venture capitalist David Sacks. He resigned earlier this year and became an external adviser to the president.

Clayton, who previously served as the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York and chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, was confirmed by the US Senate in July to oversee the nation’s spy agencies. He succeeded Bill Pulte, a controversial Trump loyalist who was appointed by the president as acting director of the US intelligence community.

It’s unclear whether Clayton would hold the role of AI tsar in addition to his duties as DNI.

“Any personnel announcement will be announced directly by the President. Any reporting until then is baseless speculation,” a White House official told Al Jazeera.

Clayton’s possible selection comes on the heels of warnings from multiple AI researchers that the technology could kill humans within a decade.

It also comes as AI giant Anthropic prepares for what is expected to be a blockbuster initial public offering (IPO), aimed for next month, and has warned that US government attitudes towards the company could impact its business.

According to an IPO prospectus seen by the Reuters news agency, the AI company said the Trump administration’s attacks and lawsuits on its technology could hurt relationships with customers and other government partners. The filing also revealed that AI could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”.

A federal appeals court ruled last week that the US government could blacklist Anthropic from US Department of Defense contracts. The court said that the agency “had ample support for its conclusion” that the company’s products pose a supply chain risk to the Pentagon and its contractors due to code that prevents them from performing certain tasks. Anthropic has said it will not allow its technology to be used for autonomous weapons or surveillance.

Anthropic’s CEO Dario Amodei and Clayton attended Tuesday’s AI meeting at the White House. Clayton was also a guest at last month’s White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Last month, Trump lashed out at Amodei over his plea for an AI slowdown, calling fears of the technology a “hoax” and a “scam”. Trump also blasted the public backlash to data centres.

Amid the public pushback against the facilities, Amazon announced on Friday that it is investing $1bn over the next five years into US communities where it operates them. Matt Garman, the CEO of the company’s cloud computing business, wrote in a blog post that the money would go towards education, job training, water preservation projects and other local priorities.

articles.title: GOP super PAC pauses spending in North Carolina Senate race, shifting money to Kansas
articles.summary: The new moves from the Senate Leadership Fund reflect a difficult landscape for Republicans, with increasingly competitive races in red states.
articles.body: A top Republican super PAC is pausing its ad spending in the Senate race in North Carolina and launching a new ad effort in Kansas, the latest sign the fight for the majority is shifting to red states amid an increasingly tough landscape for the GOP. The new moves from the Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC aligned with Senate GOP leadership, were first reported by Semafor and confirmed by two people with knowledge of the decision. Ad spending decisions can provide clear signals about the races parties and outside groups view as the most competitive and further out of reach. SLF’s move to direct resources to Kansas underscores how Democrats are putting traditionally Republican states in play as they try to net four seats to take control of the Senate. Democrats will need to win multiple states President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024, in addition to defending seats in battleground states. As Election Day draws closer, Democrats are growing more optimistic about their chances as Trump’s approval ratings drop and voters express frustrations with high costs and the Iran war. The race in Kansas between GOP Sen. Roger Marshall and Democratic pastor Adam Hamilton has become more competitive in the homestretch, even though the state has not sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. So far, SLF has reserved more than $8 million in airtime in Kansas, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. SLF had been actively involved in North Carolina, where former Republican National Committee Chairman Michael Whatley is facing former Gov. Roy Cooper, a Democrat. In September, the group spent more than $17 million on the race, according to AdImpact. The group still has another $19 million in ads booked through Election Day but now has no plans to add to that. Trump and Vice President JD Vance also each traveled to the state last month to boost Whatley, whom the president personally encouraged to run for the open seat. But the decision to pause spending in North Carolina, a perennial battleground, is a sign that the race to replace retiring Republican Sen. Thom Tillis is drifting away from the GOP. Republicans have been pessimistic for weeks about their prospects in the state, with Cooper leading in recent polling and outspending Whatley. The party’s level of confidence in their chances of defeating Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia has also been dwindling, but one person familiar with SLF’s spending noted the group has not paused its spending in that race. Trump won Georgia by just 2 points in 2024. Still, SLF has focused the bulk of its resources on other hotly contested Senate races. In September, SLF spent $78 million on ads in Texas through an affiliated group, and SLF itself spent nearly $33 million in Ohio. Elsewhere, the group last month spent $16 million in Michigan, $15 million in Iowa, $13 million in Maine, $10 million in Georgia, $8 million in Alaska and $5 million in New Hampshire, according to AdImpact. In the month of October through the Nov. 3 election, SLF’s Texas group has booked $48 million in ads, while SLF is set to spend $40 million in Ohio, $18 million in Michigan, $17 million in Maine, $16 million in Georgia, nearly $14 million in Iowa, $8 million in New Hampshire and $5 million in Alaska. Trump carried Texas, Ohio, Iowa and Alaska all by double digits in 2024. Even as SLF looks to spend its resources elsewhere, the North Carolina Senate candidates are still bracing for a hotly contested race. Whatley spokesman DJ Griffin said in a statement that Cooper recently noted Democrats are often ahead “until they’re not.” “Undecided Voters who break late decide the election in North Carolina and the majority of those Late-Breakers typically go Republican,” Griffin said. “We feel confident we have the resources to highlight Career Politician Roy Cooper’s 40 Years of Failures and win in November.” Cooper campaign manager Jeff Allen also suggested the race is still competitive, noting in a statement that a Democrat has not been elected to the Senate in North Carolina in nearly 20 years and describing North Carolina as “a 50-50 state.” “We’re building a campaign to earn every vote and make sure North Carolinians know that Roy Cooper will fight for them, while Michael Whatley will continue to enrich himself at their expense,” Allen said.

articles.title: Trump’s motorcade neared 100 mph en route to Oklahoma after helicopter, airplane ruled out
articles.summary: President Trump’s motorcade put the pedal to the metal Thursday as stormy weather in the South spurred the president to drive from rallies in Texas to Oklahoma rather than fly. Trump took the motorcade from his event at the Peterbilt Motors manufacturing plant in Denton, Texas, to his second event in Durant, Okla. The locations…
articles.body:
President Trump’s motorcade put the pedal to the metal Thursday as stormy weather in the South spurred the president to drive from rallies in Texas to Oklahoma rather than fly.

Trump took the motorcade from his event at the Peterbilt Motors manufacturing plant in Denton, Texas, to his second event in Durant, Okla. The locations are roughly 90 miles apart. Press traveling with the president noted that the vans reached speeds of 98 mph.

Typically, the president would’ve taken Marine One from Texas to Oklahoma, but stormy weather spurred the last-minute decision to drive.

During the ride to Oklahoma, Trump posted on social media that the “Beast,” or the car the president rides in, was going “faster than it has ever gone before.” “To the Great People of Oklahoma, stay tuned — I’ll be there soon! There was a major weather delay, and the planes and helicopters were not able to land, so we’re driving up from Texas,” he wrote on Truth Social . “They wanted me to postpone the event, and I said, ‘NO WAY, I’M GOING TO OKLAHOMA!’ ‘The Beast’ is going faster than it has ever gone before. It won’t be long. I love you all! See you in a little while.”

Trump showed up about two hours late in Durant, telling the crowd that he refused to cancel it entirely.

“I said, ‘What can I take?’” he told the crowd.

“I said, ‘How fast does the Beast travel?’ They said, ‘We could go close to a 100 miles per hour,’” he continued. “I said, ‘Get your a‑‑es in that car. We’re going to Oklahoma.”

Trump said he wanted to make sure he made it to Oklahoma, not because the candidates needed his help, but because he won the state all three times he ran for president.

“We got the most votes ever in the state history all three times,” he said. “And we won all 77 out of 77 counties.”
