articles.title: Wall Street Journal editorial board knocks Hegseth’s ‘weirdos’ line in speech
articles.summary: The Wall Street Journal’s conservative editorial board on Friday criticized Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s fiery comment during a Wednesday speech to active-duty officers that he wants “warriors” not “weirdos” in the military. While the opinion piece praised new initiatives introduced by the secretary during this address, including the development of autonomous warfare technology and partnering…
articles.body:
The Wall Street Journal’s conservative editorial board on Friday criticized Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s fiery comment during a Wednesday speech to active-duty officers that he wants “warriors” not “weirdos” in the military.

While the opinion piece praised new initiatives introduced by the secretary during this address, including the development of autonomous warfare technology and partnering with universities for officer recruitment, the board expressed concern that Hegseth’s “gratuitous potshots” could negatively impact recruitment efforts.

“Alas, Mr. Hegseth couldn’t resist his usual polarizing attack routine against all and sundry, and he even accused the press of ‘treason’ for publishing what’s leaking out of the secretary’s shop,” the board wrote.

“The most remembered line of the speech will be Mr. Hegseth’s declaration that the U.S. military no longer abides ‘beardos’ or ‘weirdos,’” the opinion continued. “As a practical matter, has he met anyone in defense technology lately?”

Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell defended the secretary’s speech in a statement shared with The Hill on Friday.

“Secretary Hegseth rightfully called out the Fake News media who continue to attack the achievements of our warfighters, as seen in the Wall Street Journal editorial board opinion, but their consistent smears will have no effect on the work to come,” Parnell said.

During his Wednesday speech, Hegseth revived culture-war grievances and declared the Pentagon is “no longer the woke department or the weak department.”

“Simple translation of that: No fatties, no t‑‑‑‑ies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors,” Hegseth continued, using a pejorative term for transgender people.

Alyssa Farah Griffin, a co-host of “The View” and former special assistant to President Trump, said during a Friday show she thought Hegseth’s comment was “a parody” when she first saw it posted online.

“We are the greatest fighting force in the history of mankind,” Farah Griffin said. “We’re not weak, we’re not incapable, and I don’t know where he’s hearing this from.”

Farah Griffin called the speech “bizarre” and referenced a new Republican-led effort to remove Hegseth from his role. Last month, GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.) introduced an impeachment resolution against the secretary, citing the U.S.’s ongoing military operations against Iran.

Some Republican lawmakers, including Massie, have become increasingly more outspoken against these operations as the conflict stretches into an eighth month. The House has passed three Iran war powers resolutions with the support of several Republicans, and the Senate approved a similar measure in June.

articles.body:
It’s Friday. Daylight saving time ends in less than a month unless Congress acts on pending legislation. Tell us, are you pro-daylight or standard time? 🕒

Cornell rape case now active criminal probe

Trump takes midterm push to Alabama, Ohio

Programming note : Hello! We are Steff Danielle Thomas and Colin Meyn filling in for Cate. Please send your tips, comments and story ideas to sthomas@thehill.com or cmeyn@thehill.com .

The Associated Press | Yuki Iwamura | Matt Rourke

Officials in the Empire State are taking a fresh look at the handling of an alleged gang rape at Cornell University in 2024 — and the case is now an active criminal investigation.

New York Attorney General Letitia James , whom Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) recently appointed to serve as special prosecutor in the case, discussed plans to reopen the investigation during a press conference Friday.

Hochul said the victim, identified as Jane Doe , was repeatedly “failed” by the institutions meant to protect her, raising questions about what information Cornell police shared with local prosecutors.

One key detail: The governor noted that Jane Doe told campus police she was “100 percent confident” she had been raped, but those words were not included in the account provided to prosecutors.

Despite the pressure, Hochul stopped short of calling for either Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff or the local district attorney to resign, saying she did not have enough information “at this time.” James echoed the sentiment.

Meanwhile: The governor is pushing state lawmakers to close a loophole in New York’s sexual assault law involving victims who voluntarily became intoxicated.

“Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period,” she said.

Jane Doe alleges she was drugged and gang raped by seven men at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024, but no criminal charges were filed.

She sued the university, the fraternity and others last month, bringing fresh attention to the case nearly two years later. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten subsequently reopened the investigation.

The case also sparked backlash from lawmakers and advocates for how the initial probe was handled. Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) canceled an upcoming appearance at the school over the incident.

The case is unfolding amid a larger conversation about sexual misconduct at Cornell.

The results of a 2025 campus poll found 35 percent of undergraduate women said they had experienced nonconsensual sexual contact since arriving at the university, up from 23 percent in 2023.

Overall, 15 percent of surveyed students reported such experiences, up from 11 percent two years earlier, according to a report from the school.

This really sums up President Trump ’s midterm campaign swing this week through red states he handily won in 2024.

“Campaigns and presidents don’t spend time where they’re not needed, so that is a data point,” Scott Tranter , co-founder and director of data science at Decision Desk HQ, told The Hill’s Julia Manchester .

🚚 Peterbilt truck factory outside Dallas on Thursday afternoon.

🤠 Durant, Okla., for a Thursday evening rally boosting Mike Mazzei, who’s running for governor, and Republican Rep. Kevin Hern , who is running for former Sen. Markwayne Mullin ’s seat in Senate.

No speed limit for the midterms: Trump told the crowd that his handlers told him to cancel the Oklahoma event because weather would not allow him to fly by plane or helicopter.

Trump, arriving about two hours late, said he asked how fast they could drive him to the rally.

“They said, ‘We could go close to 100 miles an hour.’ I said: ‘Get your a–es in that car. We’re going to Oklahoma,” he said as the crowd cheered, NBC News reported .

🐘 Today, Trump rallies in Mobile, Ala., which is divided between the state’s 1st and 2nd congressional districts. He’s slated to speak around 7 p.m. EDT.

House Republicans are targeting Alabama’s 2nd Congressional District, which is represented by Rep. Shomari Figures (D-Ala.), after it was redistricted to benefit Republicans. The GOP nominee, state Rep. Rhett Marques , is slated to speak at the rally.

🅾️On Saturday, Trump heads to Vandalia, Ohio, hoping to give incumbent Sen. Jon Husted a boost against former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown . In the governor’s race, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy is trailing Amy Acton in most polls.

🌽On Monday, Trump brings his tour to Nebraska for a rally with GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts , who is locked in a competitive race with Dan Osborn , an independent backed by Democrats.

Trump said in an interview published Thursday that he has not ruled out invoking the Insurrection Act or declaring a national emergency around the midterm elections in November.

“I’m not committing to anything,” he told Time , when asked about the limits of his presidential power. “We’re going to see how it plays out in court.”

The president has a history of threatening to deploy troops via the Insurrection Act of 1807, which allows the president “in all cases of insurrection, or obstruction to the laws, either of the United States, or of any individual state or territory,” to deploy members of the military or federalize members of a state’s National Guard “for the purpose of suppressing such insurrection.”

The Insurrection Act was last invoked by former President George H.W. Bush in May 1992, in response to the Los Angeles riots.

The Hill’s go-to correspondent on the 2028 Democratic beat, Amie Parnes , has a fascinating dive today into Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and how his fortunes are inevitably tied to “the other” rising progressive star, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.).

September delivered another lackluster jobs report . The U.S. added just 29,000 jobs, while unemployment edged up to 4.2 percent, according to the data .

The rearview mirror looks worse, too: July numbers were revised from a gain of 21,000 jobs to a loss of 10,000, while August was knocked down from 162,000 to 133,000.

This weak showing complicates the picture for the Federal Reserve, which raised interest rates last month for the first time in more than three years. Two competing problems: a cooling labor market and inflation that remains stubbornly above the Fed’s 2 percent target, which could open the door for another rate hike later this month.

The report also lands as Trump is already struggling to sell Americans on his economic record heading into the midterms.

A recent AP-NORC poll found just 26 percent of respondents approved of the president’s handling of the economy — a new low in the poll — while only 17 percent were keen on his policies to address the cost of living. Nearly two-thirds blamed those policies, including the energy squeeze sparked by the ongoing Iran war, for higher-than-usual prices.

🤝 Trump’s recent cozy encounters with Chinese President Xi Jinping , New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) and Big Tech leaders have some GOP strategists worried he’s dampening MAGA enthusiasm at exactly the wrong time.

🖥️ The president’s AI accord with tech leaders is also facing an early reality check. Critics warn the president’s voluntary safeguards leave too much power with the companies that are developing the technology. Insiders can read more here from The Hill’s Miranda Nazzaro .

💉 Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is in critical condition after surviving two failed lethal injection attempts earlier this week, according to her attorneys. The extraordinary ordeal is putting the death penalty — and how states carry it out — back under the microscope.

📱 More than 100 Generation Z candidates jumped into congressional races this cycle, according to Future Caucus — but few made it through their primaries. Fundraising hurdles, outsider bids and the built-in advantages of incumbency are proving tough to overcome. Read The Feed here .

📞 A Massachusetts man is facing a federal cyberstalking charge after allegedly bombarding former Trump official Katie Miller with more than 40 calls and messages. Prosecutors say he also targeted her parents and husband, White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller .

articles.title: President Trump has his camera off for G7 leader zoom
articles.summary: President Trump participated in a video-call meeting with leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) countries and the International Energy Agency (IEA) on Friday, but his camera was off while other leaders appeared on camera. Fatih Birol, executive director of the IEA, said in a post on the social platform X that leaders met to…
articles.body:
President Trump participated in a video-call meeting with leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) countries and the International Energy Agency (IEA) on Friday, but his camera was off while other leaders appeared on camera.

Fatih Birol, executive director of the IEA, said in a post on the social platform X that leaders met to discuss the global energy market and “severe pressures” on diesel supply. Birol attached a photo of the virtual meeting that showed leaders of Canada, Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom, the European Commission, France and Japan on camera while Trump was not.

It is not clear if the president’s camera was off for the entire meeting or just at the moment the picture was taken.

Birol attached a statement from the G7 leaders in which they acknowledged the volatility in oil markets and “surging prices threatening economic stability.” Diesel costs are up by more than $2 compared with a year ago, while gasoline is up by more than a dollar.

The statement said the G7 member countries, which include the U.S., would be releasing 100 million barrels of oil over the next four months with a substantial diesel release in the first 20 days. The statement condemned Iran for disrupting international trade and energy security and applauded the U.S.

“We have agreed on decisive, coordinated measures to stabilize immediate energy supplies, shield households and businesses from price shocks, and strengthen the long-term resilience of global energy systems,” the statement read.

“We commend the United States for its efforts to ensure the free flow of commerce through the Strait of Hormuz,” it added.

Trump said in a post on Truth Social on Friday morning that Europe had agreed to immediately release a “massive amount” of their diesel stockpile.

Trump has repeatedly downplayed the concerns over rising oil and gas costs and said last month that the price bump is a “very inexpensive price to pay” for what has occurred in the Iran war.

articles.title: Socialist streamer Hasan Piker faces fury after pressuring Talarico to enact far-left policy if elected
articles.summary: Hasan Piker's remarks about holding James Talarico accountable drew sharp rebukes from Ken Paxton and Ted Cruz ahead of the Texas Senate race.
articles.body: Far-left streamer Hasan Piker is getting dragged online after calling for Texas Senate nominee James Talarico to "play ball" by governing as a leftist if elected in this year's midterms. Talarico, running to be the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Texas in more than three decades, has publicly realigned on some of his more radical stances and tried to campaign on a more moderate platform despite his previous comments. But Piker, who has gained prominence through his relationship with socialist-aligned Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, appears to want Talarico to pull a bait-and-switch if he wins in November. "Hopefully, after James Talarico wins, we’ve got to hold him to account," Piker said during a campus event at the University of Texas at Austin. "We've got to make sure that he doesn’t become another, ‘do nothing Democrat’ ‘business as usual,’ and we've got to keep up that pressure. HASAN PIKER SPEAKS TO UT AUSTIN STUDENTS AFTER BACKLASH FROM TEXAS LAWMAKERS As his campaign has progressed, Talarico has rolled back on some of his controversial statements like his claim that "God is non-binary." But he continues to back progressive policies like universal healthcare, arguing his beliefs stem from "biblical grounds." Piker's recent remarks quickly became ammunition for Republicans. Talarico’s opponent, GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton, and Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, pounced, claiming that Piker is saying the quiet part out loud and showing the pressure Talarico could face from the party's left flank if he were to ascend to the U.S. Senate representing the Lone Star State. "James Talarico is bought and paid for by the Democratic Socialists," Paxton posted in response to Piker’s comments on Talarico. "And if he wins, they'll cash in at YOUR expense: raising your taxes and making life more expensive to pay for their radical agenda. Texas can't afford Talarico." Ted Cruz said on X: "When they tell you who they are…believe them." EL-SAYED TRIES TO PUT THE HASAN PIKER DEBATE BEHIND HIM AS MIDTERMS APPROACH "James Talarico will be nothing more than a puppet of the radical left," Rep. Brandon Gill, R-Texas posted. Piker erupted in the left-wing party over the past couple years, most notably campaigning with El-Sayed. Democrats, including El-Sayed, are now distancing themselves from Piker after many of his controversial statements caught heat — like his claim that "America deserved 9/11." "Hasan ‘America Deserved 9/11’ Piker expects James Talarico would support his extreme agenda & be beholden to his base," Fox News Political Analyst Guy Benson warned. "He think he’s a mafia boss, and with the psychotic state of today’s Democrat party, he’s kinda right…" Dave Rubin posted. New York City Council member Vickie Paladino said, "Hasan Piker says he’s the one actually in charge of the Democrat party." Piker’s comments, mixed with Talarico’s back-and-forth from progressive to moderate rhetoric, have sparked skepticism about the direction the Texas Democrat would take in governing if elected. "Here we have Hasan Piker—an outspoken socialist, hater of Israel and opponent of capitalism — telling us exactly what he expects from James Talarico if elected," one user posted. "He says, ‘We gotta remind [James] that we are the force that backed him…’ and got him elected and that we expect him to remember that and fall in line. Every Republican, Independent and even common-sense Democrat even thinking about voting for Talarico needs to see this and think deeply about it." "A huge reason not to vote for Talarico he has to answer to the Fascist wing of his party," another posted. "No thanks." TALARICO SAYS HE 'MISSED THE MARK' AS HE BACKTRACKS ON CONTROVERSIAL WOKE STATEMENTS Other users on social media argued Piker’s comments are irrelevant to Talarico’s campaign, and would not impact the agenda he would bring to the Senate if elected. "Hasan needs to shut the hell up," a X user named Adam Cochran posted. "He has nothing to do with Talarico’s campaign. Talarico’s campaign is the success of Talarico’s morals, policies and his hard working team’s outreach to the people of Texas." "What is Hasan even talking about," another user posted. "Talarico isn’t DSA and doesn’t owe DSA anything. He will be a senator that represents Texans, not California Socialists like Hasan." articles.title: Tony Romo, CBS part ways after DUI arrest
articles.summary: Former Dallas Cowboys quarterback and television analyst Tony Romo and CBS have parted ways after the commentator was arrested on a drunken driving charge earlier this year. Romo was placed on leave by the network following an arrest on suspicion of drunken driving in July, body camera footage of which was widely circulated on social…
articles.body:
Former Dallas Cowboys quarterback and television analyst Tony Romo and CBS have parted ways after the commentator was arrested on a drunken driving charge earlier this year.

Romo was placed on leave by the network following an arrest on suspicion of drunken driving in July, body camera footage of which was widely circulated on social media.

Footage showed Romo taking sobriety tests and talking with police officers about his history of head injuries.

“CBS Sports and Tony Romo have mutually agreed to part ways,” CBS said in a statement on Friday, according to The Athletic , which noted he had four years and more than $70 million remaining on a 10-year contract worth $180 million he signed in 2020.

After his arrest, Romo announced he would seek treatment for substance abuse and indicated it was his intention to return to the broadcast booth.

“I’m going to use this time to take a break, something I’ve never done before, and focus on my health and my family before moving on to my next opportunity,” he said in a statement shared with the outlet Friday. “I am grateful for my time with CBS Sports and for the continued support of my family and friends, as well as the NFL community and fans.”

Romo is one of the most recognizable sports media personalities in the country and has called major NFL match-ups along with longtime sportscaster Jim Nantz for CBS, including three Super Bowls.

articles.body:
Vice President Vance is headed to Alaska for a midterm rally against the backdrop of the red state’s highly competitive Senate race.

The Trump 47 Committee, a joint fundraising group connected to President Trump’s Save America PAC and the Republican National Committee (RNC), will host the Monday rally in Fairbanks, the RNC announced Friday.

With a little more than a month until Election Day, Trump and Vance are blitzing through red states — raising eyebrows as the midterm outlook looks increasingly bleak for the GOP.

The president is headed to Nebraska on Monday after stops in Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama this week. Vance was in Kansas last month and stumped this week in Florida.

Asked Wednesday whether the red state tour signals trouble for the GOP, Trump did not answer directly .

“We have the best economy anywhere in the world,” he said. “There’s no economy like this economy. The only thing we don’t have is good public relations. We don’t seem to be able to get the word across.”

In Alaska, Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is in a neck and neck race with Democrat Mary Peltola, who lost the state’s at-large House seat to Republican Rep. Nick Begich in 2024. Her moderate, Alaska-first bid has fueled Democrats’ hopes of flipping the seat in a state that’s sided with Trump in each of his three presidential races.

The Hill has reached out to Sullivan’s campaign for comment.

Alaska has elected a Democrat to the Senate just once in the last 50 years, but the Cook Political Report rates this year’s race as a toss-up. Decision Desk HQ gives Peltola a 60 percent chance of flipping the seat.

articles.title: Obama judge halts Trump firing bid as decades-old legal authority tees up possible major reversal
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's firing of court-appointed U.S. attorney Roger Rogoff was blocked by Judge Stanley Bastian, sparking a separation of powers clash.
articles.body: An Obama-appointed judge blocked President Donald Trump from firing court-appointed U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Washington Roger Rogoff, ordering the Justice Department to recognize Rogoff as the rightful officeholder and restore his ability to serve. "This is yet another ruling from an activist judge trying to thwart President Trump’s agenda and undermine his constitutional authority. U.S. attorneys serve at the pleasure of the President," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. Judge Stanley Bastian, who was first nominated by Obama in 2013, issued a preliminary injunction reinstating Rogoff and barring the administration from treating him as having been lawfully removed. The ruling sets up a legal fight over whether a president can fire a U.S. attorney appointed by federal judges. A 1979 Justice Department opinion and a 2000 federal appeals court ruling both concluded that the president has that authority. "We disagree with the decision and intend to seek an immediate stay and will appeal," the DOJ Rapid Response account wrote. TRUMP ADMIN FIRES US ATTORNEY IN SEATTLE MINUTES AFTER HE WAS APPOINTED Some legal experts and conservative attorneys took to social media to sharply criticize the ruling, arguing it infringes on the president's constitutional authority over the executive branch. "Another lawless and dangerous ruling. Violating the separation of powers. By another Democrat activist judge. This time? Seattle Obama Judge Stanley Bastian," wrote Article III founder and president Mike Davis. "Democrat judges handpicked their own U.S. attorney. The President, through his attorney general, fired him. Under Article II of the Constitution, the President clearly has the executive power to fire Justice Department officials," Davis added. Davis also noted Bastian’s first name was misspelled in the order, missing the "e" in Stanley. 'ROGUE' OBAMA JUDGE'S SMACKDOWN OF TRUMP ELECTION RULES PROVOKES OMINOUS WARNING FROM WHITE HOUSE DEPUTY "The Federal Judge misspelled his own name in his order. That's how you know it's quality legal work," wrote one user. "Now Judge Bastian created an unnecessary constitutional crisis by essentially ordering a coup at the Justice Department, by ordering the removal of the President’s pick and putting in Bastian’s judicial puppet. The Ninth Circuit must fix this. Or the Supreme Court will have to step in. Again," Davis concluded. "The President's power to remove U.S. Attorneys must be unfettered consistent with Article II of the Constitution. Judge Stanley Bastian is wrong here to order Rogoff reinstated. I predict Judge Bastian will eventually be reversed, whether at the Ninth Circuit or by the Supreme Court," said Oversight Project litigation vice president Jeff Clark. WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER "Judicial overreach, plain and simple. The judiciary does not get to run the Executive Branch. Period," said Holtzman Vogel partner Brian Nieves. In Myers v. United States (1926), which centered on President Woodrow Wilson's firing of a postmaster without Senate consent, the Supreme Court ruled that the president generally has constitutional authority to remove executive branch officers. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP More recently, the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel concluded in a 1979 opinion that the president’s statutory authority to remove "each United States attorney" also extends to prosecutors appointed by federal judges. The case is the latest in a string of legal fights over President Trump's U.S. attorney appointments, following similar disputes in New Jersey, Virginia and New York. A similar dispute unfolded in New Jersey after the administration sought to keep Alina Habba leading the U.S. attorney’s office after her interim term ended. Federal courts ultimately rejected the administration’s effort to maintain her authority, although the judges’ original appointee, Desiree Grace, did not simply take over the office. Rogoff’s case goes a step further, directly testing whether a president can remove a U.S. attorney appointed by federal judges under the statutory process for filling a vacancy.

articles.title: Another former GOP governor backs Hamilton over Marshall for Kansas Senate
articles.summary: Former Kansas Gov. Mike Hayden (R) became the second former GOP governor to support Democrat Adam Hamilton over Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) in November’s Kansas Senate race. Hayden, who served from 1987 to 1991, published an op-ed in The Wichita Eagle on Friday endorsing Hamilton for a seat that has not been held by a…
articles.body:
Former Kansas Gov. Mike Hayden (R) became the second former GOP governor to support Democrat Adam Hamilton over Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) in November’s Kansas Senate race.

Hayden, who served from 1987 to 1991, published an op-ed in The Wichita Eagle on Friday endorsing Hamilton for a seat that has not been held by a Democrat for nearly a century. He believes Hamilton will press for relief and real solutions and will listen to constituents.

“I ran for office for the first time when I was only 28 years old because I felt the person representing my community in the legislature was failing to fight for the needs of our state,” Hayden said. “Today, I am endorsing Adam Hamilton for the U.S. Senate for the same reasons.”

Former Kansas Gov. Bill Graves (R) also endorsed Hamilton last month over his party’s nominee. He said Marshall had “turned his back” on Kansas and that Hamilton knows how to “disagree without being disagreeable.”

The Kansas Senate race is likely to be won by Marshall, according to a prediction by Decision Desk HQ , but it is seen as a potentially competitive seat in an election predicted to favor Democrats.

An Emerson College poll conducted in September had Hamilton leading within the margin of error, indicating a tight race in the deep-red state.

Hamilton said in a post to the social media platform X that he is honored to have the former governor’s support.

He noted that Hayden has worked “tirelessly” for the people of Kansas and practiced the kind of leadership that is needed to make a difference.

“He knows how to put party and politics aside to deliver for working families, and I am so honored to have him by my side as I strive to do the same,” Hamilton wrote.

articles.title: Justice Department sues Maryland over federal agent mask ban
articles.summary: The Justice Department sued Maryland on Thursday over a new law barring federal law enforcement officers from wearing masks and requiring them to identify themselves while working in the Old Line State. The complaint, filed the same day the law took effect, argues that Maryland and two of its largest counties are illegally attempting to…
articles.body:
The Justice Department sued Maryland on Thursday over a new law barring federal law enforcement officers from wearing masks and requiring them to identify themselves while working in the Old Line State.

The complaint , filed the same day the law took effect, argues that Maryland and two of its largest counties are illegally attempting to regulate federal officers, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers, and are therefore violating the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause.

The new state law prohibits federal, state and local law enforcement officers from wearing face coverings while on duty, with exceptions for certain operations and protective equipment.

It also requires officers to display identification on the outermost layer of their clothing and, when asked, verbally identify themselves.

Officers who violate either requirement can face civil fines of up to $1,500, according to the complaint.

The Justice Department is challenging similar restrictions in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties. Prince George’s County’s law carries steeper penalties, allowing officers who violate its requirements to face a misdemeanor charge, up to six months in jail and a fine of up to $5,000.

“The Federal Government, not state and local governments, gets to decide which equipment federal officers may or may not wear when performing their official duties,” Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said Thursday.

The department argued masks and limits on displaying officers’ personal identities can protect federal agents from harassment and doxing and prevent suspects from identifying officers involved in future enforcement operations.

The complaint cites several incidents involving federal officers in Maryland, including an August case in which a Baltimore-area deportation officer and the officer’s spouse were doxed online.

The administration made clear in the complaint that it does not intend to follow the restrictions.

“Federal law enforcement agents and officers cannot and will not comply with the Challenged Laws, which are unconstitutional and recklessly disregard officer safety, public safety, and federal operational needs,” Justice Department attorneys write.

articles.title: Grassley calls on Trump administration to ban kratom ‘NOW’
articles.summary: Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) on Friday called on the Trump administration to finalize its proposed rule limiting the sale of kratom, a plant with opioid-like properties that can be bought over the counter. “All Kratom is deadly it should NOT be sold at gas stations/vape stores/ANYWHERE Admin needs 2 put out final 7OH rule NOW…
articles.body:
Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) on Friday called on the Trump administration to finalize its proposed rule limiting the sale of kratom, a plant with opioid-like properties that can be bought over the counter.

“All Kratom is deadly it should NOT be sold at gas stations/vape stores/ANYWHERE Admin needs 2 put out final 7OH rule NOW Kratom is killing our kids BEWARE of special interest snake oil,” Grassley said on the social media platform X .

Grassley was referring to the Drug Enforcement Administration’s (DEA) proposed rule published in July that would temporarily schedule any kratom products as Schedule 1 substances if they contain more than 0.05 percent dry weight of 7-hydroxymitragynine, or 7-OH, the opioid-like chemical found in kratom.

While currently not scheduled at the federal level, 11 states have banned it. Kratom is still legal for purchase in Iowa.

The DEA said in July that 7-OH “presents severe risks to public health, including tolerance, dependence and addiction.”

Kratom, or Mitragyna speciosa, originates from Southeast Asia. The plant is not currently scheduled under the Controlled Substances Act.

The plant is anecdotally touted as being helpful for addicts weaning themselves off opioids, but addiction organizations like American Addiction Centers do not endorse it because of the risk of dependence, a lack of regulation and potential drug interactions.

Overdoses and deaths connected to kratom are rare, though the substance was thrown back in the news last month after two University of Mississippi students were found dead near packages of kratom. It is currently unclear whether kratom was linked to their deaths, though two individuals have been charged for selling kratom in connection to the deaths.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in March published a report finding that between 2015 and 2025, kratom-related exposure reports rose by 1,200 percent.

articles.title: Dems demanding Venezuela brief face State Dept fury as senators leave town without answers
articles.summary: Senate Democrats challenge the legality of a Pentagon equity stake in Venezuelan oil company NABEP, but the State Department fires back sharply.
articles.body: The State Department is accusing Democrats of performative "grandstanding" by demanding a sweeping Venezuela oil deal briefing then postponing so the Senate could leave town early. Four senior Senate Democrats demanded documents they already knew were coming, according to material reviewed by Fox News Digital — and then the Senate rescheduled a congressional briefing on the agreement planned for Oct. 1, 2026, so they could break for fall recess. The group of lawmakers were seeking more information on the Pentagon's involvement in an agreement with North American Blue Energy Partner (NABEP) that gives the Department of War a 35% stake in one of Venezuela’s largest oil producers. State says the lawmakers had known for weeks that administration officials planned to brief the Senate Foreign Relations Committee and provide documents on the deal on Thursday. The department went forward with delivering copies of the U.S. government’s strategic partnership agreement with NABEP to the committee, claiming it did so despite the briefing being pulled down "as a courtesy." TRUMP TOUTS ACCESS TO 65 BILLION BARRELS OF VENEZUELAN OIL IN DEAL HE SAYS WILL SLASH GAS PRICES "Copies of the USG Strategic Partnership Agreement with NABEP for your Members are in the SFRC front office," a senior State Department official wrote. "Each Member has a folder with their copy." State Department Assistant Secretary for Global Public Affairs Dylan Johnson claimed Senate Democrats canceled the briefing so they could "skip town and go on vacation." "This is pure grandstanding," Johnson wrote on X. "When they sent this letter, they had known for weeks that we planned to brief them and provide the documents today, on October 1." A congressional source familiar with the planned briefing disputed State’s characterization, telling Fox News Digital that lawmakers had not been told the written NABEP agreement would be provided before writing the letter and that the briefing was intended as a broader update on U.S. policy toward Venezuela, not specifically the oil deal. And emails reviewed by Fox News Digital show the briefing postponement request itself came from a Republican majority staffer on the Foreign Relations Committee, who told State early Oct. 1 that "the Senate has left town" and asked to move the briefing until November. A State Department official told Fox News Digital the staffer was acting on behalf of the full committee. The congressional source said Republican leadership had ended legislative business for the week, with senators on both sides of the aisle preparing to leave Washington ahead of next month’s midterm elections. The group of Democrat lawmakers demanding the briefing are challenging the legality and prudence of the Trump administration’s agreement with NABEP, which would give the Pentagon rights to a 35% stake in one of Venezuela’s largest oil producers. Under the arrangement, the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital would receive rights to the stake through so-called penny warrants, while the State Department would receive preferential rights to purchase 20% of the company’s production at cost. The unusual structure is part of the administration’s broader effort to revive Venezuelan oil production and expand U.S. economic influence after Nicolás Maduro’s ouster. Democrats argue the Pentagon may lack legal authority to take the stake and have raised questions about the administration’s vetting of NABEP and its leadership. The administration argues the structure could generate substantial returns for the U.S. without requiring taxpayers to buy the stake up front. The White House has said the government’s 35% position could ultimately be worth hundreds of billions of dollars in equity and dividends if NABEP succeeds in developing the fields. The deal could also give Washington a new source of relatively low-cost crude at a time when the administration is trying to increase global supply and bring down fuel prices. State would have the right to buy 20% of NABEP’s production at cost and the right of first refusal on the remaining output, which the administration says could help replenish the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and supply U.S. military and other sensitive needs. The White House also says millions of barrels of additional Venezuelan production could eventually flow through U.S. refineries and be developed using American drilling equipment and infrastructure, generating investment and jobs in the United States. NABEP currently produces roughly 220,000 barrels a day and has said it plans to more than double production to 500,000 barrels a day by late 2028. The administration is betting that private investment can revive fields that have suffered years of underinvestment and mismanagement. The agreement is part of a much broader U.S. effort to remake Venezuela’s economy following the dramatic removal of Nicolás Maduro earlier this year. On Jan. 3, U.S. forces carried out a military operation in Venezuela to capture Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, and transport them to the United States to face federal charges. The administration has characterized the operation as a law-enforcement mission supported by the military and has since made rebuilding Venezuela’s oil sector a central part of its stabilization strategy. Interim leader Delcy Rodríguez, Maduro’s former vice president, has remained in power while cooperating with Washington, even as Venezuela’s political transition remains unsettled and opposition figures continue pressing for elections. The White House has described the NABEP agreement as part of a three-part strategy of stabilization, reconstruction and eventual democratic transition, arguing that restoring oil production is necessary to rebuild Venezuela’s economy and reduce the influence of China, Russia and other U.S. adversaries in its energy sector. TRUMP 'SERIOUSLY CONSIDERING' PLAN TO MAKE VENEZUELA AND ITS $40 TRILLION IN OIL PERMANENT PART OF USA Sens. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H.; Jack Reed, D-R.I.; Martin Heinrich, D-N.M.; and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., challenged both the legality and prudence of the deal in a letter to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, War Secretary Pete Hegseth and Energy Secretary Chris Wright. Among their central questions is whether the Pentagon office being used to structure the investment has the legal authority to acquire an equity position in a foreign oil company. The senators also demanded the agreement itself, details about how State would pay for oil and information about the administration’s vetting of NABEP and its leadership. "The proposed agreement is unlikely to reduce high energy costs for Americans, and it risks undermining the Venezuelan people’s transition away from a dictatorship," the senators wrote. Fox News Digital reached out to the offices of all four senators who signed the letter for comment. The unusual Pentagon role has drawn scrutiny since the deal was announced. Rather than immediately purchasing shares with taxpayer money, the Office of Strategic Capital’s position is structured through penny warrants that give the government the right to acquire equity for a nominal price. The Democratic senators argue that structure does not resolve the underlying legal question. They contend the statute establishing the Office of Strategic Capital authorizes loans and loan guarantees but does not explicitly empower the Pentagon to acquire equity stakes in private foreign companies. "It is unclear," the lawmakers wrote, "why the American public should support this attempt to entangle the United States with a relatively unknown foreign oil company that lacks the capacity or credibility to develop oil fields of the magnitude described." The senators also raised concerns about NABEP chairman Alejandro Betancourt, noting past money-laundering investigations involving the Venezuelan businessman. Betancourt has not been charged with a crime, and Rubio has previously said he is not under active U.S. investigation.
